topics.name: Werner's Theory & Basic Terminology
topics.summary: Alfred Werner proposed that metals show two kinds of valence: primary valence (ionizable, satisfied by negative ions, corresponds to the oxidation state) and secondary valence (non-ionizable, fixed in number, corresponds to the coordination number and points in a definite direction giving the complex its geometry). A coordination entity is an ion or neutral molecule made up of a central metal atom/ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules called ligands, written inside square brackets. The coordination number (CN) is the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central atom by sigma bonds (polydentate ligands are counted by the number of donor atoms they contribute, not by the number of ligand molecules). Ligands are classified as unidentate, didentate (bidentate), polydentate, ambidentate (can bond through either of two different donor atoms, e.g. –SCN/–NCS) and chelating (a polydentate ligand forming a ring with the metal). A complex is homoleptic if it has only one kind of ligand and heteroleptic if it has more than one kind.
key_formulas: Coordination number = number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the central atom
Primary valence → oxidation number; Secondary valence → coordination number
Denticity: unidentate = 1 donor atom, didentate = 2, polydentate = many

worked_example.q: What is the coordination number of the central metal ion in [Co(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>?
worked_example.a: Ethylenediamine (en) is a didentate ligand, contributing 2 donor N atoms each. With three en molecules the coordination number is 3 × 2 = 6, not 3.

common_mistakes: Counting the number of ligand molecules instead of the number of donor atoms when a polydentate ligand is present
Confusing primary valence (oxidation state) with secondary valence (coordination number)
Treating every metal-containing salt as a coordination compound without checking whether the metal ion loses its identity in solution

topics.name: Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds
topics.summary: IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds follows a fixed order: in a salt, the cation is named before the anion. Within a coordination entity, ligands are named first, in alphabetical order (the multiplying prefix is ignored while alphabetizing), followed by the name of the central metal. Anionic ligands take the suffix –o (chloro, cyano, oxalato, nitrito); neutral ligands mostly keep their usual name with a few exceptions (aqua for water, ammine for ammonia, carbonyl for CO, nitrosyl for NO). Simple ligands use di, tri, tetra as multiplying prefixes; ligands whose name already contains di/tri (like ethylenediamine) or whose name is complex use bis, tris, tetrakis with the ligand name in enclosing marks. The oxidation state of the central metal is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately after its name. If the complex ion is an anion, the metal name takes the suffix –ate.
key_formulas: Order: cation before anion; within the entity, ligands (alphabetical) before metal
Anionic ligand suffix: –o; anionic complex suffix on metal: –ate
Multiplying prefixes: di/tri/tetra (simple ligand); bis/tris/tetrakis (complex or di/tri-containing ligand name)

worked_example.a: Six ammine ligands (neutral) are named first with the prefix hexa-, then the metal cobalt with its oxidation state, +3, written as (III), then the anion chloride: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.

common_mistakes: Naming the metal before the ligands, or naming the anion before the cation
Using di/tri instead of bis/tris for a ligand name that already contains di/tri, such as ethylenediamine
Forgetting the –ate suffix on the metal name when the whole coordination entity is an anion

topics.name: Isomerism – Structural
topics.summary: Structural isomers of coordination compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms. Ionisation isomers differ in which ion is inside the coordination sphere and which is the counter ion outside, so they give different ions in solution and give different qualitative tests, e.g. [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br. Linkage isomers arise only with ambidentate ligands (such as –NO<sub>2</sub>/–ONO or –SCN/–NCS) that can bind through either donor atom. Coordination isomerism occurs in salts made of both a complex cation and a complex anion, where the distribution of ligands between the two metal centres can be interchanged. Solvate (hydrate) isomerism arises from the way solvent molecules (usually water) are distributed between the coordination sphere and the space outside it, which changes the number of free counter ions and hence properties like colour and conductivity.
key_formulas: Ionisation isomers: interchange of an ion between coordination sphere and counter-ion position
Linkage isomers: possible only with ambidentate ligands (–NO2/–ONO, –SCN/–NCS)
Coordination isomers: ligand-swap between a complex cation and a complex anion in the same salt

worked_example.a: They have the same molecular formula, but Br<sup>−</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> exchange positions between the coordination sphere and the counter-ion site, so they are ionisation isomers; the first gives a precipitate with BaCl<sub>2</sub> and the second gives a precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>.

common_mistakes: Calling any pair of isomers with different colours a case of linkage isomerism without checking whether an ambidentate ligand is present
Confusing ionisation isomerism (ion exchanged with a counter ion) with coordination isomerism (ligands exchanged between two complex ions)
Assuming hydrate isomers must have identical conductivity even though the number of free ions produced differs

topics.name: Isomerism – Stereoisomerism (Geometrical & Optical)
topics.summary: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of ligands. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism occurs in square planar complexes of type MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> and MABXY, and in octahedral complexes of type MA<sub>4</sub>B<sub>2</sub>, MA<sub>3</sub>B<sub>3</sub> (fac/mer) and MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>. Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because all four positions around the metal are equivalent and adjacent to one another, so only one arrangement is possible. Optical isomerism arises when a complex is chiral, i.e. its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it; this is common in octahedral complexes containing didentate ligands. For an octahedral complex such as [CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, the cis form is chiral (optically active, exists as d and l forms) while the trans form possesses a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.
key_formulas: Square planar MA2B2, MABXY and octahedral MA4B2, MA3B3, MA2B2C2 can show cis/trans isomerism
Tetrahedral complexes: no geometrical isomerism (all positions equivalent/adjacent)
cis-[MA2(AA)2] type octahedral complexes are chiral; trans- form has a plane of symmetry and is achiral

worked_example.q: Does [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] show geometrical isomerism, and does either isomer show optical isomerism?
worked_example.a: It is a square planar MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> complex, so cis and trans forms exist. Both the cis and trans square-planar isomers possess a plane of symmetry, so neither is optically active.

common_mistakes: Expecting geometrical isomerism in a tetrahedral complex just because it has two kinds of ligands
Assuming every cis isomer of an octahedral complex is automatically optically active without checking for a plane of symmetry
Mixing up fac (three like ligands on one triangular face) and mer (three like ligands in a meridian) for MA3B3 octahedral complexes

topics.name: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) – Hybridization & Geometry
topics.summary: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the geometry of a complex through the hybridization of the metal's (n-1)d, ns and np orbitals used to accept ligand electron pairs. sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization gives a tetrahedral shape; dsp<sup>2</sup> gives square planar; sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (using outer, ns-shell d orbitals) gives an octahedral, high-spin, outer orbital complex; and d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> (using inner, (n-1)d orbitals) gives an octahedral, low-spin, inner orbital complex. Strong field ligands force the pairing of the metal's own d electrons, freeing inner d orbitals for hybridization (inner orbital/low-spin complex); weak field ligands do not force pairing, so outer d orbitals must be used (outer orbital/high-spin complex). VBT successfully rationalises geometry and, indirectly, magnetic behaviour, but it cannot explain the colour of complexes, cannot quantitatively predict the exact magnitude of magnetic moments, and gives no explanation for why some ligands are 'strong' and others 'weak'.
key_formulas: sp3 → tetrahedral; dsp2 → square planar
sp3d2 (outer d) → octahedral, high spin/outer orbital complex
d2sp3 (inner d) → octahedral, low spin/inner orbital complex

worked_example.q: What hybridization and geometry does [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> adopt, and is it paramagnetic?
worked_example.a: CN<sup>−</sup> is a strong field ligand; it forces pairing of the Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) electrons, leaving one empty (n-1)d orbital that combines with one s and two p orbitals to give dsp<sup>2</sup> hybridization and a square planar shape. With all electrons paired, the ion is diamagnetic.

common_mistakes: Assuming every 4-coordinate complex is tetrahedral without checking whether the ligand field forces dsp2/square planar geometry
Forgetting that VBT hybridization type (inner vs outer orbital) depends on whether the ligand is strong or weak field
Using VBT to try to explain the colour of a complex, which VBT is not equipped to do

topics.name: Crystal Field Theory – Splitting & Colour
topics.summary: Crystal Field Theory (CFT) treats ligands as point negative charges that repel the metal's d orbitals unequally. In an octahedral field, the two orbitals pointing directly at the ligands (d<sub>z<sup>2</sup></sub>, d<sub>x<sup>2</sup>-y<sup>2</sup></sub>, called e<sub>g</sub>) are raised in energy while the three orbitals pointing between the ligands (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>, called t<sub>2g</sub>) are lowered; the energy gap is the crystal field splitting energy, Δ<sub>o</sub>. In a tetrahedral field the splitting pattern is inverted (e below t<sub>2</sub>) and the splitting Δ<sub>t</sub> is only about 4/9 of Δ<sub>o</sub> for the same ligands and metal. The relative ligand field strength is summarised by the spectrochemical series: I<sup>−</sup> < Br<sup>−</sup> < SCN<sup>−</sup> < Cl<sup>−</sup> < F<sup>−</sup> < H<sub>2</sub>O < NH<sub>3</sub> < en < CN<sup>−</sup> < CO. Colour in most transition metal complexes arises from a d-d transition, an electron absorbing a visible-light photon of energy Δ<sub>o</sub> to jump from t<sub>2g</sub> to e<sub>g</sub>; the colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed. Complexes with d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> configurations have no d-d transition available and are typically colourless/white.
key_formulas: Octahedral splitting: eg (higher) – t2g (lower), gap = Δo
Tetrahedral splitting: e (lower) – t2 (higher); Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo
Colour observed = complementary of the colour absorbed in the d-d transition

worked_example.q: Why is [Ti(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> coloured while [Sc(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is colourless?
worked_example.a: Ti<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>1</sup>, so its single electron can absorb a visible photon and jump from t<sub>2g</sub> to e<sub>g</sub>, giving a violet colour. Sc<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>0</sup>, with no d electron available to make such a transition, so the ion is colourless.

common_mistakes: Thinking that the ligand pushes d orbital energies down and up by equal, unrelated amounts rather than being a single splitting Δ measured between the two sets
Assuming a d10 ion must be coloured just because it is a transition-metal ion
Forgetting that Δt is intrinsically smaller than Δo for the same ligand set, not larger

topics.name: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
topics.summary: Whether a complex is high spin or low spin depends on a competition between the crystal field splitting energy (Δ<sub>o</sub>) and the pairing energy (P) needed to force two electrons into one orbital. If Δ<sub>o</sub> > P (strong field ligand), electrons pair up in the lower t<sub>2g</sub> set first, giving a low-spin complex with fewer unpaired electrons; if Δ<sub>o</sub> < P (weak field ligand), electrons occupy all five d orbitals singly before any pairing (Hund's rule dominates), giving a high-spin complex. This distinction only matters for d<sup>4</sup> to d<sup>7</sup> configurations in an octahedral field; d<sup>1</sup>–d<sup>3</sup>, d<sup>8</sup>, d<sup>9</sup> and d<sup>10</sup> have only one possible arrangement regardless of field strength. The number of unpaired electrons (n) is related to the experimentally measured magnetic moment by the spin-only formula μ = √n(n+2) Bohr Magnetons (BM); a complex with zero unpaired electrons is diamagnetic, and one with any unpaired electrons is paramagnetic.
key_formulas: Spin-only magnetic moment: μ = √n(n+2) BM
Strong field (Δo > P) → low spin, pairing in t2g first; Weak field (Δo < P) → high spin
Spin-state ambiguity exists only for d4–d7 octahedral configurations

worked_example.q: Find the number of unpaired electrons and the spin-only magnetic moment of [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (Co<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>6</sup>; F<sup>−</sup> is a weak field ligand).
worked_example.a: F<sup>−</sup> is weak field, so the d<sup>6</sup> configuration is high spin: t<sub>2g</sub><sup>4</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>, giving 4 unpaired electrons. μ = √4(4+2) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.

common_mistakes: Applying high-spin/low-spin reasoning to a d3 or d8 ion, which has only one possible arrangement
Confusing the pairing energy comparison direction, e.g. saying strong field ligands give high spin
Using n = number of d electrons instead of number of unpaired d electrons in the spin-only formula

topics.name: Stability of Coordination Compounds
topics.summary: The thermodynamic stability of a complex in solution is expressed through its stability (formation) constant, K, for the stepwise or overall reaction of the metal ion with ligands; a larger K means a more stable complex, and the instability (dissociation) constant is simply 1/K. Stability depends on the charge and size of the central metal ion (a smaller, more highly charged ion has a higher charge density and binds ligands more strongly), on the basicity/donor strength of the ligand, and strongly on the chelate effect: a complex with chelating (polydentate, ring-forming) ligands such as ethylenediamine or EDTA is markedly more stable than the analogous complex with a comparable number of monodentate ligands, mainly due to favourable entropy changes on chelation. Stepwise stability constants (K<sub>1</sub>, K<sub>2</sub>, K<sub>3</sub> ...) generally decrease in magnitude as more ligands are added, because of statistical and electrostatic factors.
key_formulas: Instability constant = 1/Stability constant (K)
Higher charge + smaller size of metal ion → higher charge density → greater stability
Chelate effect: polydentate/ring-forming ligands give markedly higher stability than equivalent monodentate ligands

worked_example.q: Why is [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> more stable than [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> even though both provide six Ni–N bonds?
worked_example.a: Ethylenediamine is a didentate, chelating ligand that forms stable five-membered rings with Ni<sup>2+</sup>, giving a large positive entropy gain (fewer separate particles in solution after complexation) compared with six independent ammonia molecules. This chelate effect makes the en complex considerably more stable.

common_mistakes: Assuming stability constant and instability constant are two independent, unrelated quantities rather than reciprocals
Overlooking the chelate effect and predicting equal stability whenever the number and type of donor atoms is the same
Assuming stepwise stability constants always increase as more ligands add on

topics.name: Organometallic Compounds
topics.summary: Organometallic compounds contain at least one direct metal–carbon bond. They are broadly classified as sigma-bonded (e.g. Grignard reagents, R–MgX, alkyl/aryl compounds with a single metal–C sigma bond), pi-bonded (ligands such as alkenes or arenes donate electron density from a pi system, e.g. Zeise's salt K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(η<sup>2</sup>-C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)], historically the first organometallic compound made, and ferrocene, Fe(C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, a 'sandwich' compound), and sigma-and-pi-bonded, exemplified by metal carbonyls. In a metal carbonyl such as Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> (tetrahedral), Fe(CO)<sub>5</sub> (trigonal bipyramidal) or Cr(CO)<sub>6</sub> (octahedral), CO first donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal (a sigma bond) and the metal then back-donates electron density from a filled d orbital into an empty antibonding pi* orbital of CO (pi back-bonding); this synergic sigma-donation/pi-back-donation strengthens the M–C bond while weakening (lengthening) the C–O bond.
key_formulas: Organometallic compound: contains at least one M–C bond
Classification: sigma-bonded (RMgX), pi-bonded (Zeise's salt, ferrocene), sigma+pi-bonded (metal carbonyls)
Metal carbonyl synergic bonding: CO→M sigma donation + M→CO(π*) back donation

worked_example.q: In metal carbonyls, what happens to the C–O bond length as pi back-bonding from the metal increases?
worked_example.a: Back-donation places electron density into the antibonding π* orbital of CO, which weakens the C–O bond and increases (lengthens) the C–O bond distance, while at the same time strengthening the M–C bond.

common_mistakes: Calling any metal-containing organic compound 'organometallic' even when there is no direct M–C bond
Assuming CO bonds to the metal only through simple sigma donation and ignoring the pi back-bonding component
Mixing up the classification of ferrocene/Zeise's salt (pi-bonded) with that of metal carbonyls (sigma-and-pi-bonded)

topics.name: Importance & Applications of Coordination Compounds
topics.summary: Coordination compounds are central to biology, analysis, industry and medicine. Biologically, haemoglobin is an iron-porphyrin (heme) complex bound to the protein globin and carries oxygen in blood; chlorophyll is a magnesium complex essential to photosynthesis; vitamin B<sub>12</sub> (cobalamin) is a cobalt complex; and several enzymes, such as carbonic anhydrase, are zinc complexes. Analytically, EDTA complexometric titrations are used to estimate the hardness of water (Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Mg<sup>2+</sup>), and dimethylglyoxime (DMG) forms a characteristic scarlet-red precipitate with Ni<sup>2+</sup> used in its qualitative and quantitative detection. Industrially, silver and gold are extracted from their ores as soluble cyanide complexes such as [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, and nickel is purified via the Mond process through the volatile complex Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>. In medicine, cisplatin (cis-[Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]) is used as an anticancer drug, and EDTA is used in chelation therapy to treat heavy-metal (e.g. lead) poisoning.
key_formulas: Haemoglobin: Fe-porphyrin (heme) + globin; Chlorophyll: Mg complex; Vitamin B12: Co complex
Extraction: Ag, Au leached as [M(CN)2]-; Nickel purified via Ni(CO)4 (Mond process)
Medicine: cisplatin (anticancer), EDTA (chelation therapy for heavy-metal poisoning)

worked_example.q: Why is EDTA used in the treatment of lead poisoning?
worked_example.a: EDTA is a hexadentate chelating ligand that forms a very stable, water-soluble complex with Pb<sup>2+</sup> ions in the body. This complex is then excreted, removing the toxic metal ion from tissues; this approach is called chelation therapy.

common_mistakes: Mixing up which biologically important complex uses which metal (e.g. assigning magnesium to haemoglobin instead of iron)
Thinking DMG detects Ni2+ by oxidation-reduction rather than by forming a chelate precipitate
Assuming cisplatin's anticancer activity has nothing to do with its specific cis geometrical isomer

questions.question: According to Werner's theory, which type of valence corresponds to the oxidation state of the metal and is satisfied by negative ions?
options: Secondary valence
Primary valence
Coordinate valence
Residual valence
questions.explanation: Werner called the ionizable valence, satisfied by anions and equal to the oxidation number of the metal, the primary valence.
questions.hint: Think about which valence is ionizable in solution.
distractor_logic: Secondary valence is the fixed, non-ionizable valence that gives the geometry, not the oxidation state.
"Coordinate valence" is not a term Werner used for this concept.
"Residual valence" is not part of Werner's classification of metal valences.

questions.question: What term is used for an ion or molecule that is directly bonded to the central metal atom in a coordination entity?
options: Counter ion
Coordination polyhedron
Ligand
Homoleptic ion
questions.explanation: A ligand is any ion or molecule that donates an electron pair to and is directly bonded to the central metal atom.
questions.hint: This is the general name for the species written inside the square brackets along with the metal.
distractor_logic: A counter ion balances charge outside the coordination sphere and need not be bonded directly to the metal.
Coordination polyhedron describes the spatial arrangement of donor atoms, not an individual bonded species.
Homoleptic describes a whole complex having only one kind of ligand, not a single ligand itself.

questions.question: In the formula [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>, what is the part written inside the square brackets called?
options: Coordination sphere
Ionisation sphere
Outer sphere
Lattice sphere
questions.explanation: The central metal atom together with the ligands directly attached to it, enclosed in square brackets, is called the coordination sphere.
questions.hint: It is the unit that behaves as a single entity in solution.
distractor_logic: "Ionisation sphere" is not the standard term for this part of the formula.
"Outer sphere" refers to ions/species outside the brackets, the opposite of what is asked.
"Lattice sphere" is not a recognised term in coordination chemistry nomenclature.

questions.question: A ligand such as the thiocyanate ion, which can attach to a metal through either its sulfur atom or its nitrogen atom, is called:
options: An ambidentate ligand
A bridging ligand
A polydentate ligand
A homoleptic ligand
questions.explanation: A ligand that can coordinate through two different donor atoms is called ambidentate; thiocyanate can bind as –SCN (S-bonded) or –NCS (N-bonded).
questions.hint: The name literally suggests it can bind two ways.
distractor_logic: A bridging ligand connects two separate metal centres at once, which is a different concept from ambidentate behaviour.
Polydentate refers to a ligand donating through multiple atoms simultaneously to the same or different metals, not choosing between two options.
"Homoleptic" describes a complex, not an individual ligand's bonding behaviour.

questions.question: In naming a coordination compound, what is named first?
options: The anion
The central metal always
The ligand with the highest charge
The cation
questions.explanation: By IUPAC convention, in naming any salt (including coordination compounds), the cation is named before the anion.
questions.hint: Think of how a normal salt like sodium chloride is named.
distractor_logic: The anion is named after the cation, not first.
The metal is named after the ligands within its own coordination entity, and the entity itself may be the cation or the anion.
Naming order depends on cation/anion position, not on ligand charge.

questions.question: Which multiplying prefix is used for four identical simple (unsubstituted) ligands such as ammonia in a coordination compound name?
options: quadri
tessera
tetrakis
tetra
questions.explanation: Simple ligand names use the ordinary multiplying prefixes di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa; "tetra" is used for four ammine ligands, as in tetraamminecopper(II).
questions.hint: This is the same prefix family used for simple counting in chemical nomenclature generally.
distractor_logic: "Quadri" is not an IUPAC multiplying prefix used in coordination nomenclature.
"Tessera" is not a chemical nomenclature term.
"Tetrakis" is reserved for ligand names that are already complex or already contain di/tri/tetra.

questions.question: What suffix is added to the name of a negatively charged (anionic) ligand in IUPAC nomenclature?
options: –ic
–ium
–ate
–o
questions.explanation: Anionic ligands are named with the suffix –o, e.g. chloro (Cl<sup>−</sup>), cyano (CN<sup>−</sup>), oxalato (C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>).
questions.hint: Think of examples like "chloro" or "cyano".
distractor_logic: "–ic" is not the standard IUPAC anionic ligand suffix.
"–ium" is used for some cationic ligand names (rare cases), not the general anionic ligand suffix.
"–ate" is the suffix added to the metal name when the whole complex ion is an anion, not to a ligand name.

questions.question: When the overall coordination entity being named is an anion, what happens to the name of the central metal?
options: It is dropped entirely
It is written first, before the ligands
It takes the suffix –ate
It takes the suffix –ous
questions.explanation: If the coordination entity is negatively charged overall, the metal's name is modified by adding the suffix –ate, e.g. ferrate, cobaltate, cuprate.
questions.hint: Compare cobalt(III) chloride with a complex like potassium hexacyanoferrate(II).
distractor_logic: The metal name is always retained, in modified form, never dropped.
The metal is always named after the ligands, regardless of the overall charge of the entity.
"–ous" is used in older (non-IUPAC) nomenclature for a lower oxidation state, not for anionic complexes.

questions.question: Two coordination compounds with the same formula that give different ions in solution, because an ion has swapped between the coordination sphere and the position of a counter ion, show which type of isomerism?
options: Ionisation isomerism
Linkage isomerism
Coordination isomerism
Optical isomerism
questions.explanation: When an ion outside the coordination sphere exchanges places with a ligand inside the sphere, the compounds are ionisation isomers, and they ionise to give different ions in solution.
questions.hint: Focus on what changes: which ion is "free" versus "bonded".
distractor_logic: Linkage isomerism involves an ambidentate ligand binding through a different donor atom, not an ion changing sphere position.
Coordination isomerism involves ligand redistribution between two different complex ions in the same salt, not a simple counter-ion swap.
Optical isomerism concerns non-superimposable mirror images, unrelated to which ion is a counter ion.

questions.question: Linkage isomerism can occur only when a compound contains which type of ligand?
options: A bridging ligand
A neutral ligand
A chelating ligand
An ambidentate ligand
questions.explanation: Linkage isomers differ in the donor atom through which an ambidentate ligand (like –NO2/–ONO) is attached to the metal, so this isomerism requires an ambidentate ligand.
questions.hint: Recall which ligand type can bond through two different atoms.
distractor_logic: A bridging ligand connects two metal centres; this is unrelated to a single ligand switching its donor atom.
A neutral ligand can be ambidentate or not; being neutral is not what causes linkage isomerism.
A chelating ligand forms a ring with the metal through two or more donor atoms simultaneously; it does not by itself cause linkage isomerism.

questions.question: A salt containing both a complex cation and a complex anion, in which ligands can be interchanged between the two metal centres to give an isomer, shows:
options: Ionisation isomerism
Coordination isomerism
Geometrical isomerism
Solvate isomerism
questions.explanation: Coordination isomerism arises specifically in salts of complex cations and complex anions when the distribution of ligands between the two metal centres is interchanged.
questions.hint: This isomerism needs two separate complex ions in the same salt.
distractor_logic: Ionisation isomerism involves a simple counter ion, not a second complex ion.
Geometrical isomerism is a type of stereoisomerism about spatial arrangement, not ligand exchange between two metal centres.
Solvate isomerism involves solvent molecules moving in or out of the coordination sphere, not ligand exchange between two metals.

questions.question: Isomers that differ only in the number of water molecules directly bonded to the metal versus present as free water of crystallisation are called:
options: Linkage isomers
Coordination isomers
Geometrical isomers
Hydrate (solvate) isomers
questions.explanation: Hydrate (or, more generally, solvate) isomers differ in whether solvent molecules occupy positions in the coordination sphere or exist as free molecules outside it.
questions.hint: The classic textbook example is the CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O family of isomers.
distractor_logic: Linkage isomers differ in the donor atom of an ambidentate ligand, not in solvent placement.
Coordination isomers involve two different complex ions exchanging ligands, not water placement in a single complex.
Geometrical isomers have identical connectivity but different spatial arrangement, not a different distribution of solvent molecules.

questions.question: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism is commonly observed in square planar complexes of which general type?
options: MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>
MA<sub>4</sub>
MAB<sub>3</sub>
MA<sub>3</sub>
questions.explanation: A square planar complex of type MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> can have the two A ligands adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) to each other, giving geometrical isomers.
questions.hint: You need at least two different pairs of ligands to have a cis/trans distinction.
distractor_logic: MA4 has only one kind of ligand, so no cis/trans distinction is possible.
MAB3 has only one A ligand, so there is no pair of like ligands that can be cis or trans to each other.
MA3 (a homoleptic complex, if it existed with that stoichiometry) has only one kind of ligand and cannot show geometrical isomerism.

questions.question: In an isomer described as "cis", how are the two identical (or specified) ligands arranged relative to each other?
options: Adjacent to each other (at 90° in a square planar or octahedral complex)
Randomly distributed with no fixed relationship
Both occupying axial positions only
Directly opposite each other (at 180°)
questions.explanation: "Cis" describes ligands positioned next to each other, typically at a 90° angle in square planar or octahedral geometry.
questions.hint: Cis is the opposite arrangement to trans.
distractor_logic: Cis/trans nomenclature specifically refers to a fixed geometric relationship, not a random distribution.
Being restricted to axial positions is a specific octahedral case and is not the general definition of cis.
Ligands directly opposite each other (180°) describe the trans arrangement, not cis.

questions.question: A complex that is non-superimposable on its own mirror image is said to be:
options: Chiral (optically active)
Homoleptic
Ambidentate
Achiral
questions.explanation: A chiral molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image; such molecules exist as a pair of optical isomers and are optically active.
questions.hint: This is the general chemistry definition used for handedness in molecules.
distractor_logic: Homoleptic refers to having only one kind of ligand, unrelated to symmetry/chirality.
Ambidentate describes a ligand's ability to bind through two donor atoms, unrelated to chirality of the whole complex.
Achiral molecules can be superimposed on their mirror image, the opposite of what is described.

questions.question: Why do tetrahedral complexes of the type Mabcd (four different ligands) not show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?
options: Tetrahedral complexes are always ionic and cannot be isolated
All four positions around the metal are equivalent and mutually adjacent, so only one spatial arrangement is possible
Geometrical isomerism requires at least five ligands
Tetrahedral complexes never contain more than one type of ligand
questions.explanation: In a tetrahedral arrangement every pair of positions bears the same 109.5° relationship to each other, so there is no distinct "cis" versus "trans" arrangement possible; only one structure exists (though it can still be chiral).
questions.hint: Think about the bond angles in a tetrahedron – are any two positions ever "opposite" each other?
distractor_logic: Being ionic or covalent has nothing to do with whether geometrical isomerism is possible.
Geometrical isomerism can occur with as few as four ligand positions (square planar MA2B2); the ligand count is not the limiting factor here.
Tetrahedral complexes commonly contain more than one type of ligand (e.g. mixed-ligand tetrahedral complexes exist); that is not the reason.

questions.question: According to Valence Bond Theory, which hybridization of the metal orbitals gives a tetrahedral complex?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>
dsp<sup>2</sup>
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>
questions.explanation: One s, three p orbitals combine to give four equivalent sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally.
questions.hint: This is the same hybridization used to explain the shape of methane.
distractor_logic: dsp2 hybridization gives a square planar geometry, not tetrahedral.
d2sp3 hybridization also involves six orbitals and gives an octahedral geometry (inner orbital type).
sp3d2 hybridization involves six orbitals and gives an octahedral geometry.

questions.question: Which hybridization of the metal orbitals, according to VBT, gives a square planar complex?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>
dsp<sup>2</sup>
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>
questions.explanation: One (n-1)d, one s and two p orbitals combine to give four dsp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals arranged in a square plane.
questions.hint: This hybridization is characteristic of many d<sup>8</sup> strong-field complexes.
distractor_logic: sp3 hybridization gives a tetrahedral shape, not square planar.
d2sp3 hybridization also uses six orbitals and gives an octahedral geometry.
sp3d2 hybridization uses six orbitals, giving an octahedral geometry.

questions.question: An octahedral complex in which the metal uses outer (ns, np, nd) orbitals for hybridization, i.e. sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, is generally described as:
options: A square planar complex
An inner orbital, low-spin complex
An outer orbital, high-spin complex
A tetrahedral complex
questions.explanation: sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridization uses the outer d orbitals of the same principal quantum shell as s and p, and such complexes are typically high spin (weak field ligands).
questions.hint: "Outer" in the name refers to which d orbitals (same shell as s, p, or the shell below) are used.
distractor_logic: sp3d2 involves six hybrid orbitals and gives an octahedral shape, not square planar.
Inner orbital/low-spin complexes use (n-1)d orbitals along with ns, np, giving d2sp3 hybridization, the opposite case.
sp3d2 gives an octahedral shape (six orbitals), not tetrahedral (four orbitals).

questions.question: An octahedral complex in which the metal uses inner (n-1)d orbitals together with ns and np orbitals, i.e. d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization, is generally described as:
options: A tetrahedral complex
An outer orbital, high-spin complex
A linear complex
An inner orbital, low-spin complex
questions.explanation: d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization uses inner (n-1)d orbitals, which become available only when the ligand field is strong enough to force pairing of the metal's d electrons; such complexes are low spin.
questions.hint: "Inner" refers to using the (n-1)d shell rather than the outer nd shell.
distractor_logic: d2sp3 uses six hybrid orbitals and gives an octahedral shape, not tetrahedral (four orbitals, sp3).
Outer orbital/high-spin complexes use sp3d2 hybridization with outer nd orbitals, the opposite case.
A linear complex would involve only two ligand positions (sp hybridization), unrelated to d2sp3.

questions.question: In an octahedral crystal field, which set of d orbitals is raised in energy (points directly toward the ligands)?
options: t<sub>2g</sub> (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>)
Both sets are raised equally
Neither set changes energy
e<sub>g</sub> (d<sub>z<sup>2</sup></sub>, d<sub>x<sup>2</sup>-y<sup>2</sup></sub>)
questions.explanation: The e<sub>g</sub> set (d<sub>z<sup>2</sup></sub> and d<sub>x<sup>2</sup>-y<sup>2</sup></sub>) points directly at the six ligands along the axes and is destabilised (raised in energy) in an octahedral field.
questions.hint: Think about which orbital lobes point straight along the x, y, z axes where the ligands sit.
distractor_logic: The t2g set points between the axes, away from the ligands, and is lowered in energy, not raised.
The two sets are split unequally by definition – that unequal splitting, Δo, is the whole basis of crystal field theory.
Both sets do change energy relative to the free-ion (spherical field) energy; that change is the origin of crystal field splitting.

questions.question: What is the energy gap between the t<sub>2g</sub> and e<sub>g</sub> sets of d orbitals in an octahedral field called?
options: Pairing energy, P
Ionisation energy
Lattice energy
Crystal field splitting energy, Δ<sub>o</sub>
questions.explanation: The energy separation between the two sets of d orbitals in an octahedral field is the crystal field splitting energy, denoted Δ<sub>o</sub> (or 10Dq).
questions.hint: This is the quantity that determines whether a complex is high spin or low spin.
distractor_logic: Pairing energy is the energy cost of placing two electrons in the same orbital, a separate quantity that is compared with Δo.
Ionisation energy refers to removing an electron from a gaseous atom/ion, unrelated to orbital splitting in a complex.
Lattice energy refers to the energy of an ionic crystal lattice, unrelated to d-orbital splitting.

questions.question: The colour of most transition metal complexes arises mainly from which phenomenon?
options: A d-d electronic transition
Combustion of the ligand
Radioactive decay
Nuclear magnetic resonance
questions.explanation: An electron absorbing a visible-light photon and being promoted from the lower (t<sub>2g</sub>) to the higher (e<sub>g</sub>) set of d orbitals – a d-d transition – is responsible for the colour of most transition metal complexes.
questions.hint: This transition needs partially filled d orbitals.
distractor_logic: Ligand combustion would destroy the compound, not explain its colour.
Radioactive decay is unrelated to the ordinary chemical colour of coordination compounds.
NMR involves nuclear spin transitions in a magnetic field and has nothing to do with visible colour.

questions.question: Complexes of metal ions with a d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> configuration are typically:
options: Paramagnetic
Colourless or white
Intensely coloured
Radioactive
questions.explanation: With no d electrons (d<sup>0</sup>) or a completely filled d shell (d<sup>10</sup>), no d-d transition is possible, so such complexes are usually colourless or white (e.g. Sc<sup>3+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup>).
questions.hint: Colour from a d-d transition needs at least one, but not all ten, d electrons.
distractor_logic: d0 has no d electrons and d10 has no unpaired d electrons, so both are typically diamagnetic, not paramagnetic.
Without an available d-d transition, these ions are typically not intensely coloured (barring unrelated charge-transfer effects).
d0/d10 configuration has nothing to do with radioactivity.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: The spin-only magnetic moment of a complex is calculated from the number of unpaired electrons, n, using the formula:
options: μ = 2n BM
μ = n/2 BM
μ = √n(n+2) BM
μ = n<sup>2</sup> BM
questions.explanation: The spin-only formula for magnetic moment is μ = √n(n+2), expressed in Bohr Magnetons (BM), where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
questions.hint: This is the standard formula taught for spin-only magnetic moments.
distractor_logic: "2n" is not the correct spin-only relationship; it does not match known values such as 1.73 BM for n = 1.
"n/2" is not the correct spin-only relationship between unpaired electrons and magnetic moment.
"n squared" is not the correct spin-only formula.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: A strong field ligand generally causes the d electrons of the central metal ion in an octahedral complex to:
options: Pair up in the lower-energy t<sub>2g</sub> orbitals before occupying e<sub>g</sub>, giving a low-spin complex
Spread out singly over all five d orbitals, giving a high-spin complex
Remain unaffected in energy or spin arrangement
Leave the metal entirely, giving a d<sup>0</sup> ion
questions.explanation: A strong field ligand produces a large Δ<sub>o</sub>, greater than the pairing energy, so electrons preferentially pair in the lower t<sub>2g</sub> set rather than occupy the higher e<sub>g</sub> set singly, giving a low-spin complex.
questions.hint: Compare the size of Δo with the pairing energy P.
distractor_logic: Spreading electrons singly over all five orbitals (Hund's rule maximised) describes the weak-field, high-spin case, the opposite of a strong field ligand.
A strong field ligand does change orbital energies (creates a large Δo) and can change the spin arrangement compared with a free ion or weak field case.
Coordinating to a ligand does not remove electrons from the metal ion's d subshell.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: A weak field ligand generally leads to which type of electron arrangement in the d orbitals of an octahedral complex?
options: High spin, with maximum number of unpaired electrons consistent with Hund's rule
Complete pairing in the e<sub>g</sub> set only
Low spin, with maximum pairing
No d electrons at all
questions.explanation: Weak field ligands give a small Δ<sub>o</sub>, smaller than the pairing energy, so electrons occupy all five d orbitals singly first (Hund's rule) before pairing, giving a high-spin arrangement.
questions.hint: This is the opposite situation to a strong field ligand.
distractor_logic: Electrons fill both t2g and eg orbitals singly under Hund's rule for a high-spin case, not exclusively pair in eg.
Maximum pairing describes the low-spin, strong-field case, not the weak-field case.
A weak field ligand still coordinates a metal ion that retains its d electrons; it does not remove them.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: A coordination compound in which all the electrons in the metal's d orbitals are paired is expected to be:
options: Paramagnetic
Ferromagnetic
Diamagnetic
Radioactive
questions.explanation: With no unpaired electrons (n = 0), the spin-only magnetic moment is zero and the substance is diamagnetic, weakly repelled by an external magnetic field.
questions.hint: Recall the basic definition connecting unpaired electrons to magnetic behaviour.
distractor_logic: Paramagnetic behaviour requires at least one unpaired electron, the opposite of the fully paired case described.
Ferromagnetism is a cooperative, long-range ordering effect seen in bulk metals like iron, not a property of isolated paramagnetic complex ions.
Having paired electrons has nothing to do with radioactivity.

questions.question: The equilibrium constant for the formation of a coordination complex from a metal ion and its ligands is called the:
options: Solubility product
Equivalence constant
Stability (formation) constant
Rate constant
questions.explanation: The stability constant (or formation constant), K, measures the extent to which a complex forms from its metal ion and ligands at equilibrium; a larger K means a more stable complex.
questions.hint: This constant is specifically about complex formation equilibria, not solubility or kinetics.
distractor_logic: Solubility product (Ksp) describes the dissolution equilibrium of a sparingly soluble salt, a different type of equilibrium.
"Equivalence constant" is not a standard term in this context.
A rate constant describes reaction speed (kinetics), not an equilibrium extent.

questions.question: Complexes formed with polydentate, ring-forming (chelating) ligands are generally found to be:
options: Equally stable, with no difference
Unstable and rarely isolable
More stable than analogous complexes with monodentate ligands (the chelate effect)
Less stable than analogous complexes with monodentate ligands
questions.explanation: The chelate effect describes the observation that complexes with chelating (ring-forming) ligands are generally significantly more stable than similar complexes with monodentate ligands providing the same donor atoms.
questions.hint: "Chelate effect" is the standard name for this stability boost.
distractor_logic: The chelate effect specifically predicts a measurable stability difference, not equal stability.
Many chelate complexes (e.g. EDTA complexes) are in fact exceptionally stable and easily isolated, not unstable.
This reverses the well-established chelate effect; chelation increases, not decreases, stability.

questions.question: For a given ligand, a central metal ion with a smaller size and a higher positive charge (higher charge density) generally forms complexes of:
options: Greater stability
Stability that depends only on temperature
The same stability regardless of charge or size
Lower stability
questions.explanation: A higher charge density on the metal ion means a stronger electrostatic attraction for ligand donor atoms, generally giving a more stable complex.
questions.hint: Think in terms of simple electrostatic attraction between metal and ligand.
distractor_logic: While temperature affects equilibrium constants generally, the question is about the metal-ion-dependent trend, which is charge/size based.
Charge and size of the metal ion are well-established factors affecting stability, so stability is not independent of them.
This is the reverse of the actual trend; higher charge density typically increases, not decreases, stability.

questions.question: The instability (dissociation) constant of a complex is related to its stability constant, K, as:
options: √K
K<sup>2</sup>
K
questions.explanation: The instability constant is simply the reciprocal of the stability constant: a large stability constant corresponds to a small instability constant, and vice versa.
questions.hint: Think about what "reciprocal" relationship would make sense between stability and instability.
distractor_logic: The square root of K is not the defined relationship between these two constants.
K squared is not the defined relationship between these two constants.
Setting the instability constant equal to K itself would mean stability and instability are identical, which is not the relationship.

questions.question: An organometallic compound is defined as one that contains at least one:
options: Hydrogen bond
Metal–nitrogen bond
Metal–oxygen bond
Direct metal–carbon bond
questions.explanation: By definition, an organometallic compound has at least one bond directly between a metal atom and a carbon atom.
questions.hint: The name itself hints at the two elements that must be directly bonded.
distractor_logic: Hydrogen bonding is a weak intermolecular interaction unrelated to the metal–carbon bond criterion.
A metal–nitrogen bond, as in an ammine complex, does not by itself make a compound organometallic.
A metal–oxygen bond, as in a simple metal oxide or aqua complex, does not by itself make a compound organometallic.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic example of a sigma-bonded organometallic compound?
options: Ferrocene, Fe(C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
Zeise's salt, K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)]
A Grignard reagent, R–MgX
Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: In a Grignard reagent R–MgX, the alkyl/aryl group is bonded to magnesium through a simple, localised metal–carbon sigma bond, making it a sigma-bonded organometallic compound.
questions.hint: Which of these has a simple single-bond connection between one carbon and the metal, rather than a delocalised pi system?
distractor_logic: Ferrocene involves delocalised pi-electron donation from cyclopentadienyl rings to iron, making it pi-bonded, not simply sigma-bonded.
Zeise's salt involves pi donation from the alkene's pi bond to platinum, making it pi-bonded.
Ni(CO)4 involves synergic sigma-donation and pi-back-donation between CO and Ni, not a simple sigma-only bond.

questions.question: Ferrocene, Fe(C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, in which the iron atom sits between two parallel cyclopentadienyl rings, is described as a:
options: Double salt
Chelate compound
Sandwich compound
Homoleptic carbonyl
questions.explanation: Ferrocene's structure, with the metal atom sandwiched symmetrically between two flat cyclopentadienyl rings, gives it the classic name "sandwich compound".
questions.hint: The structural description matches the everyday word for something placed between two layers.
distractor_logic: A double salt (like a Mohr's salt-type compound) dissociates fully into simple ions in solution, unrelated to ferrocene's structure.
A chelate compound has a ligand forming a ring by binding through two or more donor atoms to one metal in a localized way; that's a different structural concept from the sandwich arrangement.
Ferrocene contains no CO ligands at all, so it is not a carbonyl compound of any kind.

questions.question: Which compound is historically recognised as the first organometallic compound to be prepared, an alkene-platinum complex?
options: Mond's nickel carbonyl, Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>
Ferrocene, Fe(C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
Zeise's salt, K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)]
Grignard reagent, CH<sub>3</sub>MgI
questions.explanation: Zeise's salt, K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(η<sup>2</sup>-C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)], containing an ethylene molecule pi-bonded to platinum, is historically regarded as the first organometallic compound made.
questions.hint: This complex is named after the chemist who first prepared it in the 1820s.
distractor_logic: Ni(CO)4 was discovered later than Zeise's salt and is used in nickel purification, not credited as the first organometallic compound.
Ferrocene was discovered much later (1950s) and is not the historically "first" organometallic compound.
Grignard reagents, though very important synthetically, were developed later and are not credited as the first organometallic compound prepared.

questions.question: Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in blood, is a coordination complex of which metal?
options: Zinc
Iron
Magnesium
Cobalt
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin contains a heme group, an iron-porphyrin coordination complex, bound to the protein globin; the iron centre reversibly binds oxygen.
questions.hint: This is the metal responsible for the red colour of blood.
distractor_logic: Zinc is found in enzymes such as carbonic anhydrase, not in haemoglobin.
Magnesium is the metal found in chlorophyll, not haemoglobin.
Cobalt is the metal found in vitamin B12 (cobalamin), not haemoglobin.

questions.question: Chlorophyll, the pigment central to photosynthesis in plants, is a coordination complex of which metal?
options: Cobalt
Iron
Copper
Magnesium
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is a magnesium-containing coordination complex built on a porphyrin-like ring system, essential for capturing light energy in photosynthesis.
questions.hint: This metal is also known for its role in green plant pigments.
distractor_logic: Cobalt is the metal found in vitamin B12, not chlorophyll.
Iron is the metal found in haemoglobin, not chlorophyll.
Copper is found in some other biological complexes (e.g. haemocyanin), but not chlorophyll.

questions.question: EDTA is used in medicine as a chelating agent to treat poisoning by which type of substance?
options: Vitamin deficiencies
Bacterial toxins
Viral infections
Heavy (toxic) metals, such as lead
questions.explanation: EDTA forms very stable, water-soluble chelate complexes with toxic heavy-metal ions such as Pb<sup>2+</sup>, allowing them to be excreted from the body; this is called chelation therapy.
questions.hint: Think about EDTA's general chemical role as a strong, hexadentate chelating ligand for metal ions.
distractor_logic: EDTA is not used to correct vitamin deficiencies; that is unrelated to its metal-chelating role.
EDTA is not an antibacterial agent and does not treat bacterial toxins.
EDTA has no antiviral action.

questions.question: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>], is clinically important as:
options: An antibiotic
An anticancer drug
A vitamin supplement
An antihistamine
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a well-known platinum-based coordination compound used as a chemotherapy drug to treat several types of cancer.
questions.hint: This is one of the most cited pharmaceutical applications of coordination chemistry.
distractor_logic: Cisplatin does not act as an antibiotic against bacterial infections.
Cisplatin is not a vitamin supplement; it is a cytotoxic chemotherapy agent.
Cisplatin is not used to treat allergic reactions as an antihistamine.

questions.question: What is the coordination number of cobalt in [Co(en)<sub>3</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>, where en = ethylenediamine?
questions.explanation: Ethylenediamine is didentate (2 donor N atoms per molecule). With three en ligands, the coordination number is 3 × 2 = 6.
questions.hint: Count donor atoms, not the number of ligand molecules.
distractor_logic: 9 overcounts by treating each en as contributing 3 donor atoms; en has only 2 nitrogen donor atoms.
3 would be correct only if en were counted as a single-point (unidentate) donor, which it is not.
2 would correspond to a single en molecule's donor atoms, ignoring that three en molecules are present.

questions.question: FeSO<sub>4</sub>.(NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O (Mohr's salt) gives a positive test for Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions in solution, while K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] does not give a test for free Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions. This difference shows that Mohr's salt is a:
options: Coordination compound, while K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] is a double salt
Homoleptic complex, while K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] is heteroleptic
Chelate, while K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] is not
Double salt, while K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] is a coordination compound
questions.explanation: In a double salt like Mohr's salt, the constituent ions (Fe<sup>2+</sup>, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>) dissociate fully and retain their identity in solution, so Fe<sup>2+</sup> tests positive. In K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>], Fe is locked inside the complex [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> and does not give a free Fe<sup>2+</sup> test, marking it as a true coordination compound.
questions.hint: The key distinguishing feature is whether the metal ion loses its identity in solution.
distractor_logic: This reverses the identification; the compound that dissociates fully and shows the free metal-ion test is the double salt, not the coordination compound.
Homoleptic/heteroleptic describes the number of kinds of ligand present, not the double-salt-versus-coordination-compound distinction being tested.
This scenario is not about chelation at all; Mohr's salt contains no chelating ligand, and the distinction being drawn is double salt vs. coordination compound.

questions.question: What is the oxidation state of chromium in the complex [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>?
questions.explanation: Water is a neutral ligand, so it contributes no charge. The complex ion [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> balances three Cl<sup>−</sup> ions, so the chromium oxidation state must be +3.
questions.hint: Balance the overall charge: three chloride ions means the complex cation carries +3 charge, entirely from the metal since water is neutral.
distractor_logic: +2 would only balance two chloride ions, not three.
0 would mean the compound is completely neutral overall with no counter ions at all, which contradicts the three Cl- ions present.
+6 would require a much higher overall positive charge than the three Cl- counter ions actually balance.

questions.question: Which of the following complexes is heteroleptic (contains more than one kind of ligand)?
options: [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>
[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup>
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>
questions.explanation: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> contains two different types of ligand, ammonia and chloride, so it is heteroleptic.
questions.hint: Look for the complex with two different ligand types rather than just one.
distractor_logic: [Ni(CN)4]2- contains only cyanide ligands, making it homoleptic.
[Fe(CN)6]4- contains only cyanide ligands, making it homoleptic.
[Co(NH3)6]3+ contains only ammonia ligands throughout, making it homoleptic, not heteroleptic.

questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>?
options: Cobalt(III) hexaamminechloride
Hexaamminechlorocobalt(III)
Chlorohexaamminecobalt(III)
Hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride
questions.explanation: Ligands (six ammine) are named first with the prefix hexa-, followed by the metal cobalt with its oxidation state (III), and then the anion chloride, all giving "hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride".
questions.hint: Remember the overall order: ligands + metal(oxidation state), then the separate anion as a distinct word.
distractor_logic: This places the metal name before the ligand names, reversing the correct order within the coordination entity.
This wrongly folds chloride (which is an ionic counter ion here, not a ligand) into the coordination entity's name.
This places chloride (a separate counter ion) as a prefix attached to the coordination entity, which is incorrect since Cl- here is not bonded to cobalt.

questions.question: What is the correct formula for the compound named tetraamminecopper(II) sulfate?
options: [CuSO<sub>4</sub>(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>
[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]SO<sub>4</sub>
[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]
Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: "Tetraammine" means four NH<sub>3</sub> ligands bonded to copper(II) inside the coordination sphere, while sulfate is the separate counter anion balancing the +2 charge: [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]SO<sub>4</sub>.
questions.hint: The name tells you the counter ion (sulfate) is named separately, so it should sit outside the square brackets.
distractor_logic: This wrongly makes the whole formula, including sulfate, a single anionic complex, but the name gives no "-ate" ending on copper and specifies a neutral counter-ion pairing, not an anionic complex.
Placing sulfate inside the brackets would make it a ligand bonded to copper, which the name does not indicate.
Using two sulfate ions would require the copper to be +4, but copper(II) means the charge is only +2, matching one sulfate ion.

questions.question: Ethylenediamine (en) is named using the prefix "bis" instead of "di" when three of them are present, giving "tris(ethylenediamine)", because:
options: Ethylenediamine is a neutral ligand
The ligand's own name already contains "di", so "di"/"tri" cannot be used as the multiplying prefix without ambiguity
Ethylenediamine is an ambidentate ligand
Ethylenediamine coordinates through only one nitrogen atom
questions.explanation: Since "ethylenediamine" itself contains "di", using "tridi..." would be confusing, so the special multiplying prefixes bis, tris, tetrakis are used with the ligand name in enclosing marks instead.
questions.hint: Think about what would happen if you tried to say "tri-ethylenediamine" – would it be clear how many "di"s are multiplying prefixes versus part of the ligand's own name?
distractor_logic: Being a neutral ligand is true of ethylenediamine but is not the reason for using bis/tris; many neutral ligands (like ammonia) use ordinary di/tri/tetra prefixes just fine.
Ethylenediamine is not ambidentate (it does not have alternative donor atoms to choose between); ambidentate character is unrelated to prefix choice.
Ethylenediamine actually coordinates through two nitrogen atoms (it is didentate), not just one, and this denticity is not why the special prefix is used.

questions.question: In naming the neutral complex [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>], in what alphabetical order should the ligand names appear?
options: Whichever ligand has the higher formal charge is named first
Whichever ligand was added first in synthesis is named first
Ammine before chloro (a before c)
Chloro before ammine (c before a)
questions.explanation: IUPAC nomenclature requires ligands to be listed in alphabetical order by ligand name, ignoring multiplying prefixes; "ammine" (a) comes before "chloro" (c) alphabetically.
questions.hint: Alphabetize by the ligand's name itself, not by whether it is neutral or anionic.
distractor_logic: Formal charge on the ligand plays no role in the alphabetical-ordering rule for naming.
The order of naming is fixed by alphabetical convention and has nothing to do with the historical order of synthesis.
This reverses the correct alphabetical order; "a" precedes "c", so ammine should be named first, not chloro.

questions.question: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(NO<sub>2</sub>)]Cl<sub>2</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(ONO)]Cl<sub>2</sub> differ only in whether the nitrite ligand is bonded through nitrogen or oxygen. This is an example of:
options: Ionisation isomerism
Coordination isomerism
Linkage isomerism
Hydrate isomerism
questions.explanation: Since nitrite (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>) is ambidentate and can bond through N (nitro, –NO<sub>2</sub>) or O (nitrito, –ONO), compounds differing only in this donor atom are linkage isomers.
questions.hint: Focus on what specific atom of the ligand is bonded to the metal in each formula.
distractor_logic: Ionisation isomerism would require an ion swapping between the coordination sphere and a counter-ion position, but here the counter ion (Cl-) is unchanged in both formulas.
Coordination isomerism requires two separate complex ions (a complex cation and a complex anion) exchanging ligands, which is not the case here.
Hydrate isomerism concerns the placement of water molecules, but no water is involved in this pair of formulas.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs represents ionisation isomers?
options: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Cr(CN)<sub>6</sub>] and [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Co(CN)<sub>6</sub>]
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>]Cl<sub>2</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>ONO]Cl<sub>2</sub>
[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub> and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O
questions.explanation: In [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub> and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br, Br<sup>−</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> simply exchange positions between the coordination sphere and the counter-ion site, the defining feature of ionisation isomers, and they give different ions (and different precipitation tests) in solution.
questions.hint: Look for the pair where an ion appears to swap between being a ligand and being a counter ion.
distractor_logic: This pair exchanges ligands between two different complex ions (cobalt and chromium complexes), which is coordination isomerism, not ionisation isomerism.
This pair differs in the donor atom of an ambidentate ligand (N vs O of nitrite), which is linkage isomerism, not ionisation isomerism.
This pair differs in the number of water molecules inside versus outside the coordination sphere, which is hydrate (solvate) isomerism, not ionisation isomerism.

questions.question: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Cr(CN)<sub>6</sub>] and [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Co(CN)<sub>6</sub>] are examples of which type of isomerism?
options: Linkage isomerism
Ionisation isomerism
Geometrical isomerism
Coordination isomerism
questions.explanation: Here the ligands (ammine and cyanide) are redistributed between the two different metal centres (Co and Cr) that make up the complex cation and complex anion, which is the defining feature of coordination isomerism.
questions.hint: Notice that both compounds contain the same two metals and the same two sets of ligands, just swapped between the cation and the anion.
distractor_logic: Linkage isomerism involves a single ambidentate ligand changing its donor atom, not ligand redistribution between two whole complex ions.
Ionisation isomerism involves a simple ion swapping with a ligand inside a single coordination sphere, not an exchange between two separate complex ions.
Geometrical isomerism concerns spatial arrangement within one coordination sphere, not the identity of ligands attached to two different metal centres.

questions.question: The compounds [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub> (violet), [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O (grey-green) and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]Cl.2H<sub>2</sub>O (dark green) are all the same molecular formula, CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O, but differ in colour and properties. This is best explained as:
options: Optical isomerism, due to different chirality of the three complexes
Hydrate (solvate) isomerism, with water and chloride distributed differently between the coordination sphere and the crystal lattice
Linkage isomerism, due to an ambidentate water ligand
Coordination isomerism, due to two different metal centres
questions.explanation: In each formula, the total number of water and chloride units is the same, but they are distributed differently between the coordination sphere (bonded directly to Cr) and outside it (as counter ion / lattice water), which is precisely hydrate (solvate) isomerism, giving different colours since the ligand field around Cr differs.
questions.hint: Notice that the total formula CrCl3.6H2O is identical for all three, and only the split between "bonded" and "free" water/chloride changes.
distractor_logic: Optical isomerism concerns non-superimposable mirror images with the same connectivity, not a difference in how many ligands are directly bonded versus free.
Water is not an ambidentate ligand (it always binds through oxygen), so linkage isomerism does not apply here.
Only one metal (Cr) is present in all three compounds, so coordination isomerism, which requires two different complex ions, cannot apply.

questions.question: Does the square planar complex [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] show geometrical isomerism, and if so, of what type?
options: Yes, but only as fac and mer isomers
No, square planar complexes never show geometrical isomerism
Yes, it exists as cis and trans isomers (MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> type)
No, because it has only two kinds of ligands
questions.explanation: This is a square planar MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> complex, so the two ammine ligands can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) to each other, giving two geometrical isomers – the anticancer drug cisplatin is the cis form.
questions.hint: Recall the general rule for which square planar ligand patterns show cis/trans isomerism.
distractor_logic: Fac/mer isomerism applies specifically to octahedral MA3B3 complexes, not to a four-coordinate square planar MA2B2 complex.
Square planar MA2B2 and MABXY complexes do show geometrical isomerism; this option incorrectly denies that possibility.
Having exactly two kinds of ligands (two NH3 and two Cl) is precisely the condition (MA2B2) that allows cis/trans isomerism, not a reason to exclude it.

questions.question: Between cis-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and trans-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>, which one is optically active?
options: Both are optically active
Only the cis isomer
Only the trans isomer
Neither is optically active
questions.explanation: The cis isomer of [CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> lacks any plane of symmetry and is chiral, existing as non-superimposable mirror images (d and l forms), while the trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is achiral (optically inactive).
questions.hint: Check each isomer for an internal mirror plane; a molecule with such a plane cannot be optically active.
distractor_logic: Only the cis isomer is chiral; the trans isomer possesses a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.
This is backwards: the trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive, while the cis isomer is the chiral one.
The cis isomer, lacking a plane of symmetry, is in fact optically active, so it is not correct that neither isomer shows optical activity.

questions.question: How many geometrical isomers are possible for an octahedral complex of the type [MA<sub>3</sub>B<sub>3</sub>]?
options: 2 (fac and mer)
questions.explanation: An MA<sub>3</sub>B<sub>3</sub> octahedral complex can have the three A ligands occupying one triangular face (facial, fac) or lying in a meridional plane (meridional, mer), giving exactly two geometrical isomers.
questions.hint: Think about the two named arrangements typically discussed for this ligand pattern: fac and mer.
distractor_logic: 3 overcounts the possibilities; only the fac and mer arrangements are geometrically distinct for MA3B3.
Only 1 isomer would ignore the distinct fac and mer arrangements that are both geometrically possible.
4 overcounts the possibilities for this ligand pattern; MA3B3 gives exactly two geometrical isomers, not four.

questions.question: Does the tetrahedral complex ion [NiCl<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?
options: No, because it contains only one type of ligand
Yes, it shows fac and mer isomers
Yes, it shows cis and trans isomers just like a square planar MA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> complex
No, because all positions in a tetrahedral geometry are equivalent and mutually adjacent
questions.explanation: Even though this tetrahedral complex has two different ligands (Cl and Br), tetrahedral geometry has no distinction between "cis" and "trans" positions since every pair of positions is equivalent, so no geometrical isomerism arises.
questions.hint: Geometrical isomerism in tetrahedral complexes is generally not observed, regardless of how many different ligand types are present.
distractor_logic: The complex actually does contain two types of ligand (Cl and Br); the absence of geometrical isomerism here is due to the tetrahedral geometry itself, not the number of ligand types.
Fac/mer isomerism applies to octahedral MA3B3 complexes with six coordination positions, not a four-coordinate tetrahedral complex.
This wrongly extends the square-planar cis/trans concept to tetrahedral geometry, where no such distinction exists.

questions.question: What hybridization does Ni adopt in the square planar ion [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, and is the ion paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>; paramagnetic
dsp<sup>2</sup>; diamagnetic
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>; paramagnetic
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>; diamagnetic
questions.explanation: CN<sup>−</sup> is a strong field ligand; it forces pairing of the Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) electrons, freeing one (n-1)d orbital that combines with one s and two p orbitals for dsp<sup>2</sup> hybridization (square planar); with all electrons paired, the ion is diamagnetic.
questions.hint: Strong field ligands with a d8 ion typically favour a specific four-coordinate geometry with paired electrons.
distractor_logic: sp3 hybridization would give a tetrahedral, not square planar, shape, and this combination does not match the observed square planar, diamagnetic behaviour of this ion.
sp3d2 hybridization involves six orbitals and gives an octahedral shape, not the four-coordinate square planar geometry of this ion.
d2sp3 hybridization also involves six orbitals (octahedral), not the four-coordinate dsp2 arrangement seen here.

questions.question: What hybridization does Ni adopt in the tetrahedral ion [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, and is it paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
options: d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>; paramagnetic
sp<sup>3</sup>; paramagnetic
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>; diamagnetic
dsp<sup>2</sup>; diamagnetic
questions.explanation: Cl<sup>−</sup> is a weak field ligand and does not force pairing of the Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) electrons, so the metal uses one s and three p orbitals (sp<sup>3</sup>) for a tetrahedral shape, retaining two unpaired electrons and making the ion paramagnetic.
questions.hint: Weak field ligands with a d8 ion typically retain unpaired electrons in a tetrahedral arrangement.
distractor_logic: d2sp3 hybridization also involves six orbitals (octahedral), not the four-coordinate sp3 arrangement seen here.
sp3d2 hybridization involves six orbitals and gives an octahedral shape, not the four-coordinate tetrahedral geometry of this ion.
dsp2 hybridization gives a square planar, diamagnetic complex, which is the situation for the strong-field cyanide analogue, not this weak-field chloride complex.

questions.question: What hybridization and spin state does Fe adopt in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> (Fe<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>6</sup>)?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, high spin (paramagnetic)
dsp<sup>2</sup>, low spin (diamagnetic)
sp<sup>3</sup>, high spin (paramagnetic)
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>, low spin (diamagnetic)
questions.explanation: CN<sup>−</sup> is a strong field ligand; it forces all six d electrons of Fe<sup>2+</sup> to pair in the t<sub>2g</sub> set, freeing two inner (n-1)d orbitals for d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization, giving a low-spin, diamagnetic octahedral complex.
questions.hint: A strong field ligand on a d6 ion typically gives complete pairing and an inner-orbital octahedral complex.
distractor_logic: sp3d2 (outer orbital) hybridization corresponds to a weak-field, high-spin case, which is not what a strong ligand like CN- produces.
dsp2 hybridization gives a four-coordinate square planar shape, not the six-coordinate octahedral shape of this hexacyanide complex.
sp3 hybridization gives a four-coordinate tetrahedral shape, not the six-coordinate octahedral shape of this complex.

questions.question: What hybridization and spin state does Fe adopt in [FeF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (Fe<sup>3+</sup>, d<sup>5</sup>)?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>, high spin (paramagnetic)
dsp<sup>2</sup>, low spin (diamagnetic)
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, high spin (paramagnetic)
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>, low spin (diamagnetic)
questions.explanation: F<sup>−</sup> is a weak field ligand and does not force pairing of the five d electrons of Fe<sup>3+</sup>; the metal uses outer nd orbitals along with ns, np for sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridization, giving a high-spin, paramagnetic octahedral complex with five unpaired electrons.
questions.hint: A weak field ligand on a d5 ion typically keeps all five electrons unpaired in an outer-orbital octahedral complex.
distractor_logic: sp3 hybridization gives a four-coordinate tetrahedral shape, not the six-coordinate octahedral shape of this complex.
dsp2 hybridization gives a four-coordinate square planar shape, not the six-coordinate octahedral shape of this hexafluoride complex.
d2sp3 (inner orbital) hybridization corresponds to a strong-field, low-spin case, which is not what a weak ligand like F- produces.

questions.question: Based on the spectrochemical series, which of the following ligands produces the largest crystal field splitting (Δ<sub>o</sub>) with a given metal ion?
options: CN<sup>−</sup>
Cl<sup>−</sup>
H<sub>2</sub>O
I<sup>−</sup>
questions.explanation: CN<sup>−</sup> lies near the strong end of the spectrochemical series (... < H<sub>2</sub>O < NH<sub>3</sub> < en < CN<sup>−</sup> < CO), producing one of the largest splittings among common ligands.
questions.hint: Recall the order of the spectrochemical series from weak to strong field ligands.
distractor_logic: Cl- is a relatively weak field ligand, weaker than H2O and much weaker than CN-, so it does not give the largest splitting.
H2O is a moderate field ligand, weaker than CN-, so it does not give the largest splitting among these options.
I- is among the weakest field ligands in the spectrochemical series, giving one of the smallest splittings, not the largest.

questions.question: A complex that absorbs light mainly in the yellow region of the visible spectrum will appear to the eye as approximately which colour?
options: Yellow (the colour it absorbs)
Violet/blue (the complementary colour of yellow)
Colourless
Black, always
questions.explanation: The colour we observe is complementary to the colour of light absorbed; a complex absorbing yellow light transmits/reflects the complementary colour, roughly violet/blue.
questions.hint: The observed colour and the absorbed colour are complementary pairs on the colour wheel, not the same colour.
distractor_logic: This confuses the absorbed colour with the observed (transmitted/reflected) colour, which are complementary, not identical.
Absorbing light in the visible region is precisely what produces colour; it would not make the substance colourless.
Appearing black would require absorption across essentially the whole visible spectrum, not just the yellow region specifically.

questions.question: [Ti(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is coloured (violet) in solution mainly because:
options: Ti<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>1</sup>, allowing a d-d electronic transition when it absorbs visible light
Ti<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>10</sup>, giving strong colour from a filled d shell
Water is inherently a strongly coloured ligand
The compound is radioactive
questions.explanation: Ti<sup>3+</sup> has a single d electron (d<sup>1</sup>), which can be promoted from the t<sub>2g</sub> to the e<sub>g</sub> level by absorbing a visible-light photon, producing the observed violet colour through a d-d transition.
questions.hint: Check the d-electron count of Ti3+ and whether a d-d transition is possible.
distractor_logic: Ti3+ is actually d1, not d10; a filled d10 shell would in fact typically give a colourless ion since no d-d transition is possible.
Water is essentially colourless on its own; the colour here arises from the metal's d-d transition, not an intrinsic ligand colour.
