Radioactivity is unrelated to the ordinary visible colour produced by electronic transitions in coordination compounds.

questions.question: Aqueous Zn<sup>2+</sup> complexes are typically colourless. What is the best explanation?
options: Zinc does not form complexes at all
Zn<sup>2+</sup> complexes only absorb in the infrared, never in the visible region for other reasons
Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a d<sup>5</sup> configuration, which is always colourless
Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a d<sup>10</sup> configuration, so no d-d transition is possible
questions.explanation: Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a completely filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration; with no partially filled d subshell, no d-d electronic transition is possible in the visible region, so its complexes are typically colourless.
questions.hint: Check the electron configuration of Zn2+ and whether a d-d transition can occur.
distractor_logic: Zinc readily forms many complexes (e.g. with ammonia, cyanide, EDTA); the lack of colour is due to its electron configuration, not an inability to form complexes.
The specific, well-established reason is the d10 configuration preventing a d-d transition, not an unrelated claim about infrared-only absorption.
Zn2+ is d10, not d5; and a d5 configuration (e.g. high-spin Mn2+) is not "always" colourless in every case either.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: For [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (Co<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>6</sup>; F<sup>−</sup> is weak field), how many unpaired electrons are present, and what is the approximate spin-only magnetic moment?
options: 4 unpaired electrons; μ ≈ 4.90 BM
0 unpaired electrons; μ = 0 BM
6 unpaired electrons; μ ≈ 6.93 BM
2 unpaired electrons; μ ≈ 2.83 BM
questions.explanation: F<sup>−</sup> being weak field gives a high-spin d<sup>6</sup> arrangement, t<sub>2g</sub><sup>4</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>, with 4 unpaired electrons; μ = √4(4+2) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.
questions.hint: First decide whether the weak field ligand gives high spin or low spin for this d6 ion, then count unpaired electrons.
distractor_logic: 0 unpaired electrons corresponds to the low-spin case with a strong field ligand (as in [Co(NH3)6]3+), not the weak-field, high-spin case here.
6 unpaired electrons would require every d electron of a d6 ion to be unpaired, which is impossible with only five d orbitals available.
2 unpaired electrons does not correspond to either the high-spin (4 unpaired) or low-spin (0 unpaired) d6 octahedral arrangement.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: For [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (Co<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>6</sup>; NH<sub>3</sub> is a fairly strong field ligand), how many unpaired electrons are present, and is it paramagnetic or diamagnetic?
options: 0 unpaired electrons; diamagnetic
2 unpaired electrons; paramagnetic
1 unpaired electron; paramagnetic
4 unpaired electrons; paramagnetic
questions.explanation: NH<sub>3</sub> is strong enough to force a low-spin arrangement for Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>): all six electrons pair up in the t<sub>2g</sub> set (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>), leaving zero unpaired electrons, so the complex is diamagnetic.
questions.hint: This is the classic low-spin, strong-field d6 case, in contrast to the weak-field [CoF6]3- example.
distractor_logic: 2 unpaired electrons does not correspond to either possible d6 octahedral arrangement (which give either 0 or 4 unpaired electrons).
1 unpaired electron does not correspond to a d6 octahedral arrangement at all; d6 gives either 0 (low spin) or 4 (high spin) unpaired electrons.
4 unpaired electrons corresponds to the weak-field, high-spin case (as in [CoF6]3-), not this strong-field ammine complex.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: Comparing [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (tetrahedral, sp<sup>3</sup>) and [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (square planar, dsp<sup>2</sup>), which statement about their magnetic behaviour is correct?
options: Both are paramagnetic with the same number of unpaired electrons
[NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic (2 unpaired electrons); [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is diamagnetic (0 unpaired electrons)
[NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is diamagnetic; [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic
Both are diamagnetic
questions.explanation: In the weak-field tetrahedral chloride complex, Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) retains 2 unpaired electrons (paramagnetic); in the strong-field square planar cyanide complex, all electrons are paired (diamagnetic).
questions.hint: Recall that Cl- is weak field and CN- is strong field, and think about how that affects pairing for the same d8 ion in these two geometries.
distractor_logic: Both being paramagnetic with the same unpaired electron count ignores that the strong-field square-planar cyanide complex has all electrons paired.
This reverses the correct assignment; the chloride complex is the paramagnetic one and the cyanide complex is diamagnetic, not the other way around.
Both being diamagnetic would ignore the two unpaired electrons retained in the weak-field tetrahedral chloride complex.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: For [Mn(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> (Mn<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>5</sup>; CN<sup>−</sup> is strong field), what is the spin state and number of unpaired electrons?
options: High spin, 3 unpaired electrons
Low spin, 0 unpaired electrons
High spin, 5 unpaired electrons
Low spin, 1 unpaired electron
questions.explanation: With a strong field ligand, the d<sup>5</sup> configuration becomes low spin: t<sub>2g</sub><sup>5</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>, leaving just 1 unpaired electron in the t<sub>2g</sub> set.
questions.hint: For d5, work out the lowest-energy arrangement when the ligand field is strong enough to favour pairing over occupying eg.
distractor_logic: 3 unpaired electrons does not correspond to either the high-spin (5 unpaired) or low-spin (1 unpaired) d5 octahedral arrangement.
0 unpaired electrons is not possible for a d5 ion under any octahedral field, since five electrons in three t2g orbitals must leave at least one unpaired.
5 unpaired electrons is the high-spin d5 case (weak field ligand), not the strong-field, low-spin case asked about here.

questions.question: For a complex ML<sub>4</sub> formed in four successive steps with stepwise stability constants K<sub>1</sub>, K<sub>2</sub>, K<sub>3</sub>, K<sub>4</sub>, which general trend is usually observed?
options: K<sub>1</sub> < K<sub>2</sub> < K<sub>3</sub> < K<sub>4</sub> (stepwise constants generally increase)
The stepwise constants show no general pattern at all
K<sub>1</sub> > K<sub>2</sub> > K<sub>3</sub> > K<sub>4</sub> (stepwise constants generally decrease)
All stepwise constants are exactly equal
questions.explanation: Stepwise stability constants generally decrease as more ligands add on, due to statistical (fewer open sites, more product molecules can lose a ligand) and electrostatic (increasing steric/electronic crowding) factors.
questions.hint: Think about whether it becomes progressively easier or harder to add each successive ligand.
distractor_logic: This reverses the commonly observed trend; stepwise constants generally decrease, not increase, with each successive ligand addition.
There is in fact a well-recognised general pattern (a decreasing trend), so it is incorrect to say no pattern exists.
Statistical and electrostatic factors make the steps generally unequal, so the constants are not typically all equal.

questions.question: [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is found to be considerably more stable than [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, even though both provide six Ni–N bonds. What best explains this?
options: The chelate effect: en is a didentate, ring-forming ligand, giving a more favourable entropy change on complex formation
Ammonia cannot bond to Ni<sup>2+</sup> at all
Nickel changes oxidation state when en is used instead of ammonia
En is a much stronger field ligand purely due to a larger negative charge
questions.explanation: Although both give six Ni–N bonds, ethylenediamine chelates (forms rings) with the metal, releasing more free ligand molecules per mole of complex formed than the ammonia case, giving a more favourable (positive) entropy change and hence greater overall stability – this is the chelate effect.
questions.hint: Compare the number of separate particles released into solution when the analogous complex forms from six NH3 versus three en molecules.
distractor_logic: Ammonia readily forms strong complexes with Ni2+ (e.g. [Ni(NH3)6]2+ is a well-known, stable complex); it is not that ammonia fails to bond at all.
Both complexes retain Ni2+ throughout; there is no oxidation state change caused by switching the ligand from ammonia to en.
Ethylenediamine is a neutral ligand, not negatively charged, so this explanation about charge is incorrect; the real reason is the entropy-driven chelate effect.

questions.question: Fe<sup>3+</sup> complexes with a given ligand are generally more stable than the corresponding Fe<sup>2+</sup> complexes with the same ligand. What is the main reason?
options: Fe<sup>3+</sup> is a larger ion than Fe<sup>2+</sup>
Fe<sup>3+</sup> has a higher charge and therefore a higher charge density than Fe<sup>2+</sup>, giving stronger electrostatic attraction to ligand donor atoms
Fe<sup>3+</sup> always uses the chelate effect while Fe<sup>2+</sup> never does
Fe<sup>2+</sup> cannot form complexes at all
questions.explanation: A higher oxidation state generally means a smaller ionic radius and a greater positive charge, both of which increase the charge density on the metal ion and strengthen its electrostatic attraction for ligand donor atoms, increasing complex stability.
questions.hint: Recall the two related metal-ion factors (charge and size) that raise charge density.
distractor_logic: In fact, higher-charge cations of the same element are typically smaller, not larger, than their lower-charge counterparts, due to greater effective nuclear pull on the remaining electrons.
The chelate effect depends on the type of ligand used (whether it is polydentate), not on which oxidation state of iron is involved; both Fe2+ and Fe3+ can form chelates with suitable ligands.
Fe2+ readily forms many well-known complexes (such as [Fe(CN)6]4-); it is not that Fe2+ fails to complex at all.

questions.question: Given the following approximate overall stability constants (logβ) for Ni<sup>2+</sup> complexes: [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> logβ ≈ 8.6, [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> logβ ≈ 18.3. Which complex is thermodynamically more stable, and by roughly how many orders of magnitude does its stability constant exceed the other?
options: [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is more stable, by roughly 2 orders of magnitude
[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is more stable, by roughly 10 orders of magnitude
[Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is more stable, by roughly 10 orders of magnitude
Both are equally stable since logβ values are similar in scale
questions.explanation: Since logβ is a logarithmic (base-10) scale, a difference of about 18.3 − 8.6 ≈ 9.7, or roughly 10 orders of magnitude, in logβ means the en complex's stability constant is about 10<sup>10</sup> times larger – a dramatic illustration of the chelate effect.
questions.hint: Remember that logβ is a base-10 logarithm, so differences in logβ correspond to powers of ten in the actual stability constant.
distractor_logic: This understates the logarithmic gap; 18.3 − 8.6 is close to 10, not 2, orders of magnitude difference.
This correctly identifies the more stable complex but assigns the trend to the wrong species; [Ni(en)3]2+ has the larger logβ and is therefore the more stable one, not [Ni(NH3)6]2+.
A difference of nearly 10 units on a log10 scale corresponds to a huge (roughly 10-billion-fold), not negligible, difference in actual stability constants, so they are far from equally stable.

questions.question: In Zeise's salt, K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)], how does the ethylene molecule bond to platinum?
options: Through hydrogen bonding between an ethylene C–H and platinum
Through a single, localized sigma bond from one specific carbon atom
Through side-on donation of its pi (π) electron density to the metal (pi-bonded)
Through ionic bonding between an ethylene cation and platinum
questions.explanation: The alkene's filled π molecular orbital donates electron density sideways into an empty metal orbital, making ethylene a pi-bonded (side-on) ligand in Zeise's salt, historically the first recognised organometallic pi-complex.
questions.hint: Ethylene has no lone pair or single carbon suited to a normal sigma-donor bond in this complex; think about which of its molecular orbitals could donate electron density.
distractor_logic: There is no meaningful hydrogen bond between a C-H of ethylene and platinum in this complex; the bonding is through the alkene pi system.
A single localized sigma bond from one carbon would be the bonding mode of an alkyl ligand (like in a Grignard reagent), not an intact alkene bound side-on as in Zeise's salt.
Ethylene is a neutral molecule in this complex, not an ionic species, so ionic bonding does not describe this interaction.

questions.question: In a metal carbonyl such as Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>, describe the synergic bonding between CO and the metal.
options: CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal (sigma bond) while the metal back-donates electron density into an empty antibonding orbital of CO (pi back-bonding)
There is no real bond between CO and the metal; they are simply held together by van der Waals forces
CO only donates electron density to the metal, with no back-donation from the metal
The metal donates electron density to CO, but CO donates nothing back to the metal
questions.explanation: In metal carbonyls, carbon monoxide first forms a sigma bond by donating its carbon lone pair to the metal, and the metal then donates electron density from a filled d orbital into an empty antibonding π* orbital of CO; this two-way (synergic) sigma-donation/pi-back-donation strengthens the overall M–C bond.
questions.hint: "Synergic" bonding implies two complementary donation directions happening at once.
distractor_logic: Metal carbonyls involve genuine covalent (sigma and pi) bonding between the metal and carbon, considerably stronger than simple van der Waals attraction.
This describes only half of the synergic bonding picture, omitting the crucial pi back-donation from the metal into the CO antibonding orbital.
This reverses the initial sigma-donation direction; CO donates to the metal first via its carbon lone pair, and it is the metal that then back-donates.

questions.question: What are the respective geometries of Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>, Fe(CO)<sub>5</sub> and Cr(CO)<sub>6</sub>?
options: Square planar, octahedral, tetrahedral
Octahedral, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal
Linear, square planar, octahedral
Tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral
questions.explanation: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> is four-coordinate and tetrahedral, Fe(CO)<sub>5</sub> is five-coordinate and trigonal bipyramidal, and Cr(CO)<sub>6</sub> is six-coordinate and octahedral, matching the number of CO ligands on each metal.
questions.hint: Match each geometry to the coordination number implied by the number of CO ligands (4, 5, and 6 respectively).
distractor_logic: This mismatches every geometry with the wrong carbonyl (e.g. giving a four-coordinate complex a square planar rather than tetrahedral shape).
This assigns tetrahedral geometry (four-coordinate) to Cr(CO)6, which is actually six-coordinate and octahedral, among other mismatches.
None of these three carbonyls is two-coordinate (linear) or four-coordinate square planar; this distractor does not match any of the actual carbonyl coordination numbers involved (4, 5, 6).

questions.question: A Grignard reagent, R–Mg–X, is classified as which type of organometallic compound?
options: Pi-bonded
Sigma-and-pi-bonded (synergic)
Sigma-bonded
Not organometallic at all, since Mg is not a transition metal
questions.explanation: The alkyl or aryl group R is bonded to magnesium through a simple, localized metal–carbon single (sigma) bond, making Grignard reagents classic examples of sigma-bonded organometallic compounds.
questions.hint: Look at whether the bonding involves a simple single bond from one carbon, or delocalised pi-electron donation.
distractor_logic: Pi-bonded organometallics (like Zeise's salt or ferrocene) involve delocalised pi-electron donation from an unsaturated or aromatic system, not the simple single M–C bond of a Grignard reagent.
Synergic sigma-and-pi bonding is characteristic of metal carbonyls, not the simple sigma bond present in a Grignard reagent.

Organometallic compounds are defined by having a direct M–C bond regardless of whether the metal is a transition metal; magnesium (a main-group metal) still forms genuine organometallic compounds like Grignard reagents.

questions.question: How does the dimethylglyoxime (DMG) test detect Ni<sup>2+</sup> ions?
options: DMG reduces Ni<sup>2+</sup> to metallic nickel, which is then weighed
DMG acts as a chelating ligand, forming an insoluble scarlet-red complex with Ni<sup>2+</sup>
DMG oxidises Ni<sup>2+</sup> to a higher, coloured oxidation state
DMG reacts with water to release a gas that is tested
questions.explanation: Dimethylglyoxime coordinates to Ni<sup>2+</sup> through two donor atoms per molecule, forming a characteristic insoluble scarlet-red chelate complex, used both to detect and to gravimetrically estimate nickel.
questions.hint: This is a chelation (complex-formation) based test, not a redox or gas-evolution test.
distractor_logic: The test relies on complex formation and precipitation, not reduction of Ni2+ to the metal.
This is not a redox reaction; the nickel remains as Ni2+ throughout, coordinated within the chelate complex, not oxidised to a different state.
No gas is released or tested in the DMG test for nickel; the diagnostic signal is the coloured precipitate itself.

questions.question: Why are silver and gold commercially extracted from their ores using a cyanide solution?
options: Cyanide precipitates the metal as an insoluble salt directly from the solid ore
Cyanide is used only to remove impurities, not the metal itself
The metal forms a soluble complex ion, such as [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, allowing it to be leached out of the ore and later recovered
Cyanide reduces the ore directly to metal without complex formation
questions.explanation: Cyanide ions form soluble complex ions with silver and gold, such as [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, which dissolve out of the crushed ore into solution; the metal is then recovered from this solution, typically by displacement with a more reactive metal such as zinc.
questions.hint: This process relies on converting an insoluble metal in the ore into a soluble coordination complex.
distractor_logic: The whole point of using cyanide is to dissolve the metal (as a soluble complex), which is the opposite of precipitating it as an insoluble solid at that stage.
Cyanide's key role here is specifically to complex and dissolve the desired metal (Ag or Au), not simply to remove unrelated impurities.
The metal is brought into solution as a complex ion first, not reduced directly to the metal while still in the solid ore.

questions.question: In the Mond process for purifying nickel, impure nickel is converted to which volatile compound, which is later decomposed to yield pure nickel?
options: NiCl<sub>2</sub>
Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>
Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
NiSO<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: In the Mond process, impure nickel reacts with carbon monoxide to form the volatile complex Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>, which is then heated further to decompose back into pure nickel metal and CO, leaving impurities behind.
questions.hint: This intermediate compound is a well-known example of a tetrahedral metal carbonyl.
distractor_logic: NiCl2 is an ionic salt and is not a volatile coordination compound used in this purification process.
This ammine chloride complex is not the intermediate formed or used in the Mond nickel purification process.
NiSO4 is an ionic sulfate salt, not a volatile complex used in the Mond process.

questions.question: EDTA titrations are commonly used analytically to determine which property of a water sample?
options: Its pH
Its dissolved oxygen content
Its radioactivity level
Its hardness (Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup> content)
questions.explanation: EDTA is a hexadentate chelating ligand that forms very stable 1:1 complexes with Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup>; complexometric titration with EDTA is a standard method for determining water hardness.
questions.hint: This links directly to EDTA's role as a powerful chelating agent for divalent metal ions.
distractor_logic: pH is measured using acid-base indicators or a pH meter, not an EDTA complexometric titration.
Dissolved oxygen is measured by other methods (such as the Winkler method), not by EDTA complexation.
Radioactivity is measured with radiation detectors, completely unrelated to EDTA's metal-chelating chemistry.

questions.question: Consider [Pt(en)Cl<sub>2</sub>]. What is the coordination number of platinum, and is the complex homoleptic or heteroleptic?
options: Coordination number 2; heteroleptic
Coordination number 4; heteroleptic (en and Cl are different ligands)
Coordination number 4; homoleptic (all ligands count as one type)
Coordination number 3; heteroleptic
questions.explanation: Ethylenediamine (en) is didentate, contributing 2 donor N atoms, and the two Cl<sup>−</sup> ions contribute one donor atom each, giving a total coordination number of 2 + 2 = 4. Since en and Cl are different ligand types, the complex is heteroleptic.
questions.hint: Add up donor atoms from en (didentate) and Cl (monodentate) separately, then check whether more than one kind of ligand is present.
distractor_logic: This correctly gets coordination number 4 but wrongly calls the complex homoleptic; en and Cl are chemically distinct ligand types, making the complex heteroleptic, not homoleptic.
This correctly identifies the complex as heteroleptic but arrives at the wrong coordination number by not correctly summing en (2) and two Cl (2) donor atoms to get 4.
Counting en as contributing only 1 (as if it were monodentate) undercounts the coordination number; en is didentate and contributes 2 donor atoms.

questions.question: The ligand EDTA<sup>4−</sup> is hexadentate. In the complex ion [Co(EDTA)]<sup>−</sup>, what is the coordination number of cobalt contributed by this single ligand molecule?
questions.explanation: Even though only one EDTA<sup>4−</sup> ion is present, being hexadentate it wraps around the metal and donates six atoms (typically four O and two N) to the metal, giving a coordination number of 6 from this single ligand.
questions.hint: Coordination number depends on the number of donor atoms delivered, not on the number of separate ligand molecules or ions.
distractor_logic: 2 severely undercounts EDTA's denticity, which is six, not two.
Counting EDTA as contributing only 1 donor atom treats it as if it were unidentate, ignoring its hexadentate (six-donor-atom) nature.
4 undercounts EDTA's denticity; it is described as hexadentate (six donor atoms: typically 4 carboxylate O and 2 amine N), not tetradentate.

questions.question: In [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)]<sup>+</sup>, where oxalate (C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>) is a didentate ligand, what are the coordination number of Cr and its oxidation state?
options: Coordination number 5; oxidation state +3
Coordination number 4; oxidation state +2
Coordination number 6; oxidation state +1
Coordination number 6; oxidation state +3
questions.explanation: Four ammine ligands (4 donor atoms) plus one didentate oxalate (2 donor atoms) gives coordination number 4 + 2 = 6. For the overall charge: 4(0) + (−2 for oxalate) + x(Cr) = +1, so x = +3.
questions.hint: First sum donor atoms (remembering oxalate counts twice), then use overall ionic charge to back-calculate the oxidation state.
distractor_logic: Coordination number 5 undercounts by forgetting that the didentate oxalate contributes two donor atoms, not one, giving 4+1=5 instead of the correct 4+2=6.
This undercounts the coordination number (missing oxalate's second donor atom) and also miscalculates the oxidation state; the correct values are 6 and +3 respectively.
The coordination number here is correctly 6, but the oxidation state calculation is wrong; balancing charge (0 from NH3, -2 from oxalate) against the overall +1 charge requires Cr to be +3, not +1.

questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name for the neutral complex [PtCl(NO<sub>2</sub>)(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>], which contains two ammine ligands, one chloro ligand and one N-bonded nitro ligand?
options: Chloronitrodiammineplatinum(II)
Diamminenitrochloroplatinum(II)
Diamminechloronitroplatinum(II)
Dichloroamminenitroplatinum(II)
questions.explanation: Ligands are listed alphabetically by name, ignoring multiplying prefixes: ammine (a) < chloro (c) < nitro (n), giving "diamminechloronitro", followed by the metal and its oxidation state (II), calculated from the neutral overall charge with one -1 chloro and one -1 nitro balancing Pt(+2).
questions.hint: Alphabetize strictly by the first letter of each ligand's own name, ignoring "di-" and other multiplying prefixes.
distractor_logic: This places chloro before ammine, but alphabetically "ammine" (a) must come before "chloro" (c), so this ordering is incorrect.
This places nitro before chloro, but alphabetically "chloro" (c) must come before "nitro" (n), so this ordering is incorrect.
This wrongly implies two chloro ligands (di-chloro) and only one ammine, but the actual complex has two ammine ligands and only one chloro ligand.

questions.question: A student sees the IUPAC name "potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)" and must deduce the formula. Which formula is correct?
options: K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]
K<sub>3</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]
K<sub>2</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]
K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: "Ferrate(II)" means the complex anion has Fe in the +2 state; six cyanide (−1 each) plus Fe(+2) gives an overall charge of −6 + 2 = −4 on [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup>, which requires four K<sup>+</sup> ions to balance, giving K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>].
questions.hint: Work out the charge on the complex anion first from the metal's oxidation state and the six −1 cyanide ligands, then balance with the right number of K+.
distractor_logic: This would correspond to a +3 oxidation state, i.e. "ferrate(III)", not the ferrate(II) actually named.
This provides too little positive charge to balance a -4 complex anion; the anion needs four K+, not two.
This formula, with two full [Fe(CN)6] units per four K+, does not correctly represent the simple 1:1 metal-to-hexacyanide-complex stoichiometry implied by the name.

questions.question: Which of these compound names correctly uses the anionic complex suffix "–ate" only where it is actually required?
options: Potassium tetrachloridoplatinate(II) for K<sub>2</sub>[PtCl<sub>4</sub>], and hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride for [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>
Hexaamminecobaltate(III) chloride for [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>
Potassium tetrachloridoplatinum(II) for K<sub>2</sub>[PtCl<sub>4</sub>]
Both compounds should use the "–ate" suffix on the metal
questions.explanation: The "–ate" suffix is added only when the coordination entity itself is an anion: [PtCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is anionic, so "platinate" is correct, while [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is a cation, so it stays "cobalt", not "cobaltate".
questions.hint: Check the actual overall charge sign of each coordination entity (the part in square brackets) before deciding whether to add "–ate".
distractor_logic: This incorrectly adds "–ate" to cobalt even though [Co(NH3)6]3+ is a cation, not an anion; the "–ate" suffix should not be used here.
This omits the required "–ate" suffix even though [PtCl4]2- is genuinely an anionic complex, so "platinum" should have become "platinate".
Since one complex is a cation ([Co(NH3)6]3+) and the other is an anion ([PtCl4]2-), only the anionic one should take the "–ate" suffix, not both.

questions.question: A student is given two coordination compounds, both with molecular formula CoBrSO<sub>4</sub>(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>. Compound A gives a white precipitate with BaCl<sub>2</sub> (indicating free sulfate ions) but not with AgNO<sub>3</sub>; Compound B gives a precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub> (indicating free bromide ions) but not with BaCl<sub>2</sub>. What type of isomerism do A and B show, and what are their likely formulas?
options: Ionisation isomerism; A = [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub>, B = [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br
Geometrical isomerism; A is cis and B is trans
Coordination isomerism; A and B have ligands swapped between two different metals
Linkage isomerism; A and B differ in the donor atom of an ambidentate ligand
questions.explanation: Compound A releases free SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> (precipitates with BaCl<sub>2</sub>) but keeps Br<sup>−</sup> bonded to Co, so A = [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub>; Compound B releases free Br<sup>−</sup> (precipitates with AgNO<sub>3</sub>) but keeps SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> bonded, so B = [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br. This ion-for-ion swap between the coordination sphere and the counter-ion position is ionisation isomerism.
questions.hint: Work out from each precipitation test which ion (Br- or SO4 2-) is "free" (a counter ion) and which is bonded inside the coordination sphere in each compound.
distractor_logic: Geometrical isomerism concerns spatial arrangement within an unchanged coordination sphere composition, but here the actual composition of the coordination sphere itself differs between A and B (one has Br bonded, the other has SO4 bonded).
Only one metal (Co) is present in both compounds; coordination isomerism specifically requires two different complex ions (e.g. a complex cation and a complex anion), which is not the case here.
Linkage isomerism requires an ambidentate ligand switching its donor atom; neither Br- nor SO4 2- is behaving as an ambidentate ligand bound through alternative atoms here, so this does not fit.

questions.question: Two salts, [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Cr(ox)<sub>3</sub>] and [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>][Co(ox)<sub>3</sub>] (ox = oxalate, didentate), have the same overall formula but different metal-ligand pairings. Which statement correctly deduces their relationship and coordination numbers?
options: They cannot be isomers since they contain different combinations of metal and ligand
They are linkage isomers because oxalate is ambidentate
They are coordination isomers, but the cobalt-containing complex always has a coordination number of 3
They are coordination isomers, and each metal centre in both salts has a coordination number of 6
questions.explanation: Both compounds contain the same two metals (Co, Cr) and the same total ligand set (six NH<sub>3</sub>, three didentate oxalate ions), only redistributed between the cation and anion, so they are coordination isomers. In both cases, the hexaammine ion has CN = 6, and the tris(oxalato) ion has CN = 3 × 2 = 6 (oxalate is didentate), so every metal centre here has coordination number 6.
questions.hint: Check that the same overall metals and ligand set appear in both formulas, just distributed differently between the complex cation and complex anion, then compute each coordination number remembering oxalate's denticity.
distractor_logic: Having the same overall set of metals and ligands, merely redistributed between the cation and anion, is exactly the definition of coordination isomerism; it does not disqualify them from being isomers of each other.

Oxalate is not ambidentate (it does not offer alternative donor-atom choices on a single ligand); the correct isomerism classification here is coordination isomerism, since ligands are redistributed between two different complex ions.

This correctly identifies coordination isomerism but wrongly states the cobalt complex's coordination number as 3, forgetting that oxalate is didentate (3 oxalate ions give 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms, not 3).

questions.question: For the three hydrate isomers of CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O – [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub>, [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]Cl.2H<sub>2</sub>O – how many moles of free (precipitable, ionisable) chloride ions does one mole of each compound release in solution, respectively?
questions.explanation: Only the chloride ions written outside the square brackets are free (ionisable) counter ions: [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]Cl<sub>3</sub> releases all 3 Cl<sup>−</sup>; [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O has one Cl<sup>−</sup> bound to Cr and releases 2 free Cl<sup>−</sup>; [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]Cl.2H<sub>2</sub>O has two Cl<sup>−</sup> bound to Cr and releases only 1 free Cl<sup>−</sup>.
questions.hint: Only chloride ions written outside the square brackets count as free, precipitable ions; chloride bonded directly to Cr inside the brackets does not immediately precipitate with AgNO3.
distractor_logic: This assumes no free chloride in the first compound and increasing amounts after, which is incorrect; the first compound in fact releases the most free chloride (all 3), decreasing as more Cl- becomes metal-bound.
This exactly reverses the correct trend; as more Cl- moves inside the coordination sphere (bonded to Cr) across the series, fewer, not more, free Cl- ions remain outside, going 3, 2, 1, not 1, 2, 3.
This assumes all chloride is always free regardless of formula, ignoring that some Cl- is directly bonded to Cr (inside the brackets) in the second and third isomers.

questions.question: How many geometrical isomers are possible in total for an octahedral complex of the type [M(AA)<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>], where AA is a symmetrical didentate ligand?
options: 3 (cis, trans, and a third unrelated form)
1 (only one arrangement is possible)
2 (a cis and a trans form)
questions.explanation: For [M(AA)<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>], the two monodentate B ligands can be positioned cis (adjacent, at 90°) or trans (opposite, at 180°) to each other, giving exactly two geometrical isomers.
questions.hint: Focus on the relative positions of only the two B ligands; the didentate AA ligands' own geometric constraints leave exactly two distinct placements for B.
distractor_logic: There is no third, structurally distinct geometrical arrangement beyond cis and trans for this ligand pattern; a third "unrelated form" is not chemically meaningful here.
Only 1 arrangement would ignore that the two B ligands can genuinely be placed either adjacent or opposite to one another, both of which are physically realisable.
4 overcounts the geometrical possibilities; only cis and trans placements of the two B ligands are geometrically distinct for this pattern.

questions.question: For [M(AA)<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>] (M = Co, AA = en, B = Cl), how many total stereoisomers exist once optical isomerism is also taken into account, and why?
options: 2 in total: cis and trans, and neither is chiral
1 in total, since en is a symmetrical ligand and prevents any stereoisomerism
4 in total: both cis and trans exist as separate d and l pairs
3 in total: 1 achiral trans isomer, plus a chiral cis isomer that exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (d and l)
questions.explanation: The trans-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> isomer has a plane of symmetry and is achiral (1 form); the cis-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> isomer lacks such a plane and is chiral, existing as a non-superimposable d/l mirror-image pair (2 forms), giving 3 stereoisomers in total.
questions.hint: Determine geometrical isomers first (cis/trans), then separately check each one for a plane of symmetry to see if it further splits into optical isomers.
distractor_logic: This misses that the cis isomer is chiral and therefore exists as two distinct optical isomers (d and l), not just one form, undercounting the total.

En being a chelating, didentate ligand does not by itself prevent stereoisomerism; in fact, its presence in the cis arrangement here is exactly what removes the molecule's symmetry plane and creates chirality.

This wrongly doubles every geometrical isomer into an optical pair; only the cis form (lacking a symmetry plane) is chiral, while the trans form (having a symmetry plane) is not, so the total is 3, not 4.

questions.question: Why is trans-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> optically inactive, while cis-[CoCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is optically active?
options: Optical activity depends only on molecular formula, and both isomers share the same formula, so both should behave identically
The trans isomer possesses an internal plane of symmetry, making it superimposable on its mirror image, while the cis isomer lacks such a plane and is chiral
The trans isomer has a lower coordination number than the cis isomer
The cis isomer contains a different metal oxidation state than the trans isomer
questions.explanation: The two Cl ligands in the trans isomer lie directly opposite each other, and the overall arrangement possesses a mirror plane, making the molecule identical to its mirror image (achiral). In the cis isomer, no such symmetry plane exists, so the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable, making it chiral and hence optically active.
questions.hint: The key test for optical activity is the presence or absence of an internal symmetry element (like a mirror plane), not just the molecular formula.
distractor_logic: Having the same molecular formula does not guarantee identical optical behaviour; stereoisomers with identical formulas can still differ in chirality depending on their three-dimensional symmetry, exactly as seen here.
Both isomers have exactly the same coordination number (6, octahedral); coordination number is unrelated to which isomer is chiral.
Both isomers involve Co in the same oxidation state (+1 overall complex charge from the same Co(III), 2 Cl-, 2 neutral en); oxidation state is not what differs between them.

questions.question: How many geometrical isomers exist for a square planar complex of the general type [M(a)(b)(c)(d)] with four different unidentate ligands a, b, c, d?
questions.explanation: In a square planar Mabcd complex, three distinct geometrical arrangements are possible depending on which ligand is placed trans to which other ligand (a-trans-b/c-trans-d; a-trans-c/b-trans-d; a-trans-d/b-trans-c), giving 3 geometrical isomers.
questions.hint: Think about the different possible ways to pair up ligands into "trans partners" across the square plane, since each distinct pairing scheme gives a different isomer.
distractor_logic: Only 1 isomer would ignore that different trans-pairings of the four distinct ligands genuinely give distinguishable structures.
6 overcounts, since although there are 4!/ways to arrange four items, many of these arrangements are equivalent by rotation of the square plane, leaving only 3 genuinely distinct isomers.
2 undercounts the possibilities; there are three, not two, distinct ways to pair the four different ligands into trans partners in a square plane.

questions.question: An octahedral complex of Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) is experimentally found to have a magnetic moment of 0 BM (diamagnetic). Based purely on this magnetic data and VBT, which hybridization must the complex have adopted?
options: sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (outer orbital, high spin)
dsp<sup>2</sup> (square planar)
sp<sup>3</sup> (tetrahedral)
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> (inner orbital, low spin)
questions.explanation: A magnetic moment of 0 BM means all electrons are paired (0 unpaired electrons), which for a d<sup>6</sup> ion only happens in the low-spin arrangement (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>); this low-spin state corresponds to inner-orbital d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization.
questions.hint: First deduce the number of unpaired electrons from the given magnetic moment, then work out which d6 spin state (and hence hybridization) matches that number.
distractor_logic: sp3d2 (outer orbital) hybridization corresponds to the high-spin d6 case, which has 4 unpaired electrons and a large non-zero magnetic moment, not the observed 0 BM.
dsp2 hybridization describes a four-coordinate square planar complex, not a six-coordinate octahedral one, so it does not match this octahedral d6 case.
sp3 hybridization describes a four-coordinate tetrahedral complex, not a six-coordinate octahedral one, so it is not consistent with this being described as octahedral.

questions.question: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> has nickel in the zero oxidation state (Ni<sup>0</sup>, d<sup>10</sup>) and is tetrahedral and diamagnetic. Which hybridization is consistent with this, and why does the oxidation state matter here?
options: d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization; CO is a very strong field ligand so it must be low spin octahedral
sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization; with a full d<sup>10</sup> configuration, all d orbitals are already filled and paired, so no d-electron rearrangement is needed regardless of ligand field strength
dsp<sup>2</sup> hybridization; CO always forces square planar geometry
sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridization; the zero oxidation state means all valence electrons remain unpaired
questions.explanation: In the zero oxidation state, Ni has a d<sup>10</sup> configuration, which is already completely filled and diamagnetic; the four-coordinate, tetrahedral shape corresponds to sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization of the 4s and 4p orbitals, with the filled 3d<sup>10</sup> subshell not participating in bonding.
questions.hint: Work out Ni's d-electron count in the zero oxidation state first, and recall that a fully filled d subshell needs no further electron rearrangement.
distractor_logic: A d10 configuration has no partially filled d subshell available for low-spin/high-spin distinctions or for d2sp3 hybridization (which needs empty inner d orbitals); this option misapplies the concept to a filled-shell case.
CO does not force square planar geometry universally; its effect depends on the metal's d-electron count and coordination number, and here the observed geometry is tetrahedral, not square planar.

A d10 configuration is already completely filled and therefore has zero, not many, unpaired electrons; also, sp3d2 would give six-coordinate octahedral geometry, not the observed four-coordinate tetrahedral shape.

questions.question: VBT successfully predicts that [Ni(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (Ni<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>8</sup>) is paramagnetic and octahedral via sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridization, with 2 unpaired electrons. What key property of the complex can VBT alone NOT explain from this analysis?
options: Its overall geometry (octahedral shape)
Whether it is paramagnetic or diamagnetic
The coordination number of nickel in the complex
Why the complex is coloured (its d-d absorption and the specific colour observed)
questions.explanation: VBT is built around explaining hybridization, geometry and (indirectly) the number of unpaired electrons, but it has no mechanism for explaining why a complex absorbs specific wavelengths of visible light and appears coloured; that requires crystal field theory's orbital energy splitting.
questions.hint: Recall the well-known limitation of VBT compared with CFT regarding one specific observable property.
distractor_logic: VBT is specifically designed to rationalise geometry through hybridization, so it does successfully explain the octahedral shape here.
VBT does predict paramagnetism/diamagnetism via the number of unpaired electrons implied by the hybridization scheme, so this is something VBT can address, unlike colour.
The coordination number (6, from six water ligands) is directly read off the hybridization scheme (sp3d2 uses six orbitals), so VBT handles this aspect without difficulty.

questions.question: For a low-spin octahedral d<sup>6</sup> complex (electron configuration t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>), each t<sub>2g</sub> electron contributes −0.4Δ<sub>o</sub> and each e<sub>g</sub> electron contributes +0.6Δ<sub>o</sub> to the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE). What is the CFSE (ignoring pairing energy) for this configuration?
options: −2.4Δ<sub>o</sub>
−1.2Δ<sub>o</sub>
−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>
0Δ<sub>o</sub>
questions.explanation: CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>) + 0 × (+0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>) = −2.4Δ<sub>o</sub>.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of electrons in each set by its respective per-electron energy contribution and sum the two results.
distractor_logic: This corresponds to only 3 electrons in t2g (as in a high-spin d3 or the t2g3 portion of high-spin d5), not the full 6 electrons in this low-spin d6 case.
This corresponds to only 1 electron in t2g, not the full 6 electrons present in the low-spin d6 (t2g6 eg0) configuration.

0Δo would result only if the stabilisation from t2g electrons were exactly cancelled by destabilisation from eg electrons, which is not the case here since eg is empty and all six electrons are stabilised in t2g.

questions.question: For a high-spin octahedral d<sup>5</sup> complex (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>3</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>), using −0.4Δ<sub>o</sub> per t<sub>2g</sub> electron and +0.6Δ<sub>o</sub> per e<sub>g</sub> electron, what is the net CFSE?
options: +1.2Δ<sub>o</sub>
−0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>
−2.0Δ<sub>o</sub>
0Δ<sub>o</sub>
questions.explanation: CFSE = 3 × (−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>) + 2 × (+0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>) = −1.2Δ<sub>o</sub> + 1.2Δ<sub>o</sub> = 0Δ<sub>o</sub>. A high-spin d<sup>5</sup> configuration has zero net crystal field stabilisation.
questions.hint: Calculate the t2g contribution and the eg contribution separately and see if they cancel out.
distractor_logic: A positive net CFSE would mean the complex is less stable than the free ion in a spherical field with no splitting, which is not correct here; the two contributions exactly cancel to give zero, not a positive value.
This does not correctly cancel the eg contribution; recompute 3(-0.4) + 2(0.6) carefully rather than treating it as if only the t2g electrons contributed.
This would only be correct if all five electrons were in t2g (as in a hypothetical low-spin d5), but here 2 of the 5 electrons occupy the destabilised eg set, changing the total.

questions.question: Comparing low-spin [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>, CFSE = −2.4Δ<sub>o</sub>) with high-spin [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>4</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>, CFSE = −0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>), which statement correctly compares their crystal field stabilisation?
options: The ammine complex has a much larger (more negative) CFSE in terms of Δ<sub>o</sub>, consistent with NH<sub>3</sub> being a stronger field ligand that favours a low-spin state
Both complexes have exactly equal CFSE since both are d<sup>6</sup> systems
CFSE cannot be compared between complexes with different ligands
The fluoride complex has the larger (more negative) CFSE because F<sup>−</sup> is a stronger field ligand
questions.explanation: The low-spin d<sup>6</sup> arrangement (all six electrons stabilised in t<sub>2g</sub>) gives a CFSE of −2.4Δ<sub>o</sub>, considerably more stabilising (in units of Δ<sub>o</sub>) than the high-spin arrangement's −0.4Δ<sub>o</sub> (4 electrons in t<sub>2g</sub>, 2 in eg, which partly cancel); NH<sub>3</sub> is high enough in the spectrochemical series to force the low-spin state for Co<sup>3+</sup>.
questions.hint: Recompute each CFSE from its stated electron configuration and compare the magnitudes directly (both are expressed relative to the same Δo scale for comparison purposes).
distractor_logic: Although both are d6 systems, their different electron configurations (low spin vs high spin) give clearly different CFSE values in terms of Δo, so they are not equal.
CFSE values, expressed as multiples of Δo, can absolutely be compared in this relative sense between complexes with different ligands, as done in this very question.
This reverses the comparison; F- is a weak field ligand giving the high-spin, less-stabilised (in terms of Δo) arrangement, while NH3 gives the more strongly stabilised low-spin arrangement.

questions.question: The tetrahedral splitting energy is related to the octahedral splitting energy for the same metal and ligand set by Δ<sub>t</sub> ≈ (4/9)Δ<sub>o</sub>. Why does this relationship mean that essentially all tetrahedral complexes are high spin?
options: Because pairing energy is always zero in a tetrahedral field
Because tetrahedral complexes never contain d electrons
Because Δ<sub>t</sub> is so much smaller than Δ<sub>o</sub>, it is almost always smaller than the pairing energy, P, so electrons prefer to occupy all orbitals singly rather than pair up
Because tetrahedral complexes can only be formed by strong field ligands
questions.explanation: Since Δ<sub>t</sub> is only about 4/9 of the corresponding Δ<sub>o</sub>, it is rarely large enough to exceed the pairing energy P even with normally "strong" field ligands, so pairing is not favoured, and tetrahedral complexes are essentially always high spin.
questions.hint: Compare the typical size of Δt against a typical pairing energy P, given that Δt is intrinsically about 4/9 as large as Δo for the same ligand and metal.
distractor_logic: Pairing energy is a property of the metal ion's electron-electron repulsions and is not zero simply because the geometry is tetrahedral; it is still compared against the (smaller) Δt.
Tetrahedral complexes of transition metals commonly do contain partially filled d subshells (that is the whole basis for discussing their spin state); this option is factually incorrect.

Tetrahedral geometry can arise with a range of ligands, not exclusively strong field ones; the high-spin outcome instead results from Δt typically being too small relative to P, not from a restriction on which ligands can form tetrahedral complexes.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: Consider an octahedral Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) complex. Explain why [Ni(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (weak field) and a hypothetical strong-field octahedral Ni<sup>2+</sup> complex would both show the same number of unpaired electrons.
options: Nickel cannot form low-spin octahedral complexes under any circumstances
Ni<sup>2+</sup> always has zero unpaired electrons regardless of the ligand
Strong and weak field ligands always produce identical magnetic moments for every d-electron count

For a d<sup>8</sup> ion, only one arrangement (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>, with 2 unpaired electrons in eg) is possible regardless of ligand field strength, since there is no alternative way to distribute 8 electrons among 5 orbitals without leaving 2 unpaired in eg
questions.explanation: With 8 electrons distributed among 5 d orbitals in an octahedral field, the t<sub>2g</sub> set (3 orbitals) is necessarily filled first (6 electrons, all paired), leaving 2 electrons for the 2 eg orbitals; by Hund's rule these 2 electrons occupy each eg orbital singly, giving exactly 2 unpaired electrons in every case – there is no alternative low-spin arrangement possible since t2g can hold at most 6 electrons.
questions.hint: Work out the only possible way to place 8 electrons into 3 (t2g) + 2 (eg) orbitals, and see if a genuinely different (fully paired) arrangement is even possible.
distractor_logic: Nickel(II) octahedral complexes are, in fact, essentially always found to have 2 unpaired electrons because low-spin d8 octahedral is not a distinct, lower-energy alternative arrangement; this is not a blanket rule about nickel forbidding all low-spin states in general, but a consequence of the d8 electron count specifically.

Ni2+ (d8) octahedral complexes are typically paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons, not zero; a genuinely diamagnetic Ni2+ complex (0 unpaired electrons) instead requires a different, four-coordinate square-planar geometry (dsp2), not an octahedral one.

This is only true for d8 specifically, where only one distribution is geometrically possible; for other configurations like d4-d7, ligand field strength does change the number of unpaired electrons (there is a real high-spin/low-spin distinction there).

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: Compare [Mn(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> (Mn<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>5</sup>, strong field, low spin) with [MnCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> (Mn<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>5</sup>, weak field, high spin). Which has the larger spin-only magnetic moment, and what are the approximate values?
options: Both complexes have identical magnetic moments since both contain Mn<sup>2+</sup>
[Mn(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> has the larger moment, since strong field ligands always increase magnetic moment
Neither complex is paramagnetic since Mn<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>5</sup>, an especially stable half-filled configuration
[MnCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> has the larger moment: 5 unpaired electrons, μ ≈ 5.92 BM, versus 1 unpaired electron and μ ≈ 1.73 BM for the cyanide complex
questions.explanation: The weak-field chloride ligand gives a high-spin d<sup>5</sup> arrangement (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>3</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup>, 5 unpaired electrons, μ = √5(5+2) = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM), while the strong-field cyanide ligand gives a low-spin arrangement (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>5</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>, 1 unpaired electron, μ = √1(1+2) = √3 ≈ 1.73 BM); the chloride complex has the larger moment.
questions.hint: Work out the spin state (high or low spin) for each ligand separately, count unpaired electrons in each, and then apply the spin-only formula to compare.
distractor_logic: Sharing the same metal ion and d-electron count (d5) does not guarantee the same magnetic moment; the ligand field strength changes the spin state and hence the number of unpaired electrons and magnetic moment, as shown by the contrasting 5.92 BM and 1.73 BM values.

This reverses the correct relationship: strong field ligands promote pairing, which generally decreases (not increases) the number of unpaired electrons and hence the magnetic moment, as seen here with the low-spin cyanide complex having the smaller moment.

d5 half-filled stability refers to the extra exchange stabilisation of a high-spin d5 free ion/weak-field complex, not an absence of paramagnetism; both complexes here are in fact paramagnetic, just to different degrees (5 vs 1 unpaired electrons).

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: For octahedral complexes with a d<sup>4</sup> to d<sup>7</sup> metal ion, why does the ligand field strength (weak vs strong) create a real spin-state ambiguity, whereas for d<sup>8</sup>, d<sup>9</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> octahedral complexes it does not?
options: Ligand field strength only affects ions with an odd number of d electrons
d<sup>8</sup>–d<sup>10</sup> ions cannot form octahedral complexes at all

For d<sup>4</sup>–d<sup>7</sup>, the electrons can either occupy eg singly (Hund's rule, high spin) or pair up in t<sub>2g</sub> instead (low spin), giving two genuinely different possible arrangements, whereas for d<sup>8</sup>–d<sup>10</sup> the t<sub>2g</sub> set is already full (6 electrons) so any additional electrons must occupy eg with no alternative arrangement available
d<sup>4</sup>–d<sup>7</sup> ions are always paramagnetic, while d<sup>8</sup>–d<sup>10</sup> ions are always diamagnetic, by definition
questions.explanation: With 4 to 7 electrons, the t<sub>2g</sub> set (holding up to 6 electrons) is not yet completely filled, so there is a genuine choice between adding the next electron to an empty/singly occupied eg orbital (high spin) or pairing it into a partially filled t<sub>2g</sub> orbital (low spin); once you reach 8 or more electrons, t<sub>2g</sub> is necessarily full (6 electrons, all paired) and any further electrons have no choice but to occupy the eg set, removing the ambiguity.
questions.hint: Track exactly how many electrons are needed to completely fill the three t2g orbitals, and see for which total electron counts a real "choice" of orbital still exists.
distractor_logic: Spin-state ambiguity is governed by whether t2g is already completely filled, not by whether the electron count is odd or even; for instance, both even (d4, d6) and odd (d5, d7) counts in this range show high-spin/low-spin possibilities.

Octahedral complexes of d8, d9 and d10 metal ions are well known and common (e.g. [Ni(H2O)6]2+ is d8 octahedral); the lack of spin-state ambiguity is due to the t2g set being full, not an inability to form octahedral complexes.

This overgeneralises; among d4-d7, whether the complex is paramagnetic and to what degree still depends on high spin vs low spin (they are not "always" one fixed type), and some d8-d10 complexes (with unpaired eg electrons, e.g. octahedral d8 or d9) are in fact paramagnetic, not always diamagnetic.

questions.topic: Crystal Field Theory – High Spin/Low Spin & Magnetic Properties
questions.question: A coordination compound is measured to have a spin-only magnetic moment of approximately 4.90 BM. What is the most likely number of unpaired electrons, and which of the following configurations is consistent with this value?
options: 2 unpaired electrons, consistent with a low-spin d<sup>8</sup> square planar ion
4 unpaired electrons, consistent with a high-spin octahedral d<sup>6</sup> ion such as high-spin Fe<sup>2+</sup> or Co<sup>3+</sup> with a weak field ligand
0 unpaired electrons, since 4.90 BM indicates a diamagnetic substance
5 unpaired electrons, consistent with any d<sup>5</sup> ion regardless of ligand field
questions.explanation: Using μ = √n(n+2), for n = 4, μ = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM, matching the given value; this level of unpaired spin is consistent with a high-spin d<sup>6</sup> octahedral ion (weak field ligand), such as high-spin Fe<sup>2+</sup> or Co<sup>3+</sup>, in a t<sub>2g</sub><sup>4</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>2</sup> arrangement.
questions.hint: Solve √n(n+2) ≈ 4.90 for the integer n that fits, then match n to a plausible d-electron configuration.
distractor_logic: 2 unpaired electrons would give μ = √8 ≈ 2.83 BM, not the observed 4.90 BM, so this configuration does not match the given magnetic moment.
A magnetic moment of 0 BM (not 4.90 BM) would indicate a diamagnetic substance with zero unpaired electrons; a substantial non-zero moment like 4.90 BM instead indicates significant paramagnetism.

5 unpaired electrons would give μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM, not 4.90 BM, so this does not match the given value, and in any case a d5 ion's spin state does depend on ligand field strength (it is not fixed "regardless").

questions.question: For a series of complexes [MX<sub>6</sub>]<sup>n−</sup> with the same ligand X but different central metal ions, stability generally increases with metal ions of higher charge density (higher charge, smaller radius), and further increases if the ligand is a strong Lewis base (highly basic donor atom). Using both these factors, which complex would be predicted to be the most stable: (i) a large, singly charged metal ion with a weakly basic ligand, (ii) a small, triply charged metal ion with a strongly basic ligand, (iii) a large, singly charged metal ion with a strongly basic ligand, or (iv) a small, triply charged metal ion with a weakly basic ligand?
options: (ii): small, triply charged metal ion combined with a strongly basic ligand
(iii): large, singly charged metal ion combined with a strongly basic ligand
All four combinations would give identical stability since only the number of ligands matters
(i): large, singly charged metal ion combined with a weakly basic ligand
questions.explanation: Both factors favour stability independently: a small, highly charged metal ion has high charge density (attracts ligand donor atoms strongly), and a strongly basic ligand donates electron density more readily; combining both factors in the same complex (option ii) gives the greatest predicted stability, since neither favourable factor is missing.
questions.hint: Check each combination against both stability factors (metal charge density and ligand basicity) and see which one has both factors working in its favour simultaneously.
distractor_logic: This combination only has the favourable ligand factor but pairs it with a low-charge-density metal ion, so its predicted stability is only partial, not maximal.
Stability constants are well known to vary substantially with both metal-ion charge/size and ligand basicity, not just with the number of ligands present, so this option's premise is incorrect.
This combination has neither favourable factor (low charge density metal ion and a weak donor ligand), so it would be predicted to be among the least stable, not the most stable.

questions.question: Why is [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> considerably more stable (has a much larger stability constant) than [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, even though both have Fe<sup>2+</sup> as the central ion and neither uses a chelating ligand?
options: CN<sup>−</sup> is a much stronger field/stronger donor ligand than H<sub>2</sub>O, forming stronger metal-ligand bonds (with significant pi back-bonding contribution), which raises the stability constant even without any chelate effect
Stability constants only depend on the charge of the metal ion, so they should actually be equal here
The chelate effect is responsible for the difference, since CN<sup>−</sup> is secretly a didentate ligand
Water cannot form a stable complex with Fe<sup>2+</sup> under any circumstances
questions.explanation: In the absence of any chelate effect (both ligands here are monodentate), stability differences arise from intrinsic ligand-donor strength; CN<sup>−</sup> is a much stronger field ligand than H<sub>2</sub>O, forming a stronger covalent metal-ligand interaction (including pi back-bonding into CN<sup>−</sup>'s empty orbitals), which is reflected in a substantially higher stability constant.
questions.hint: Since chelation is not a factor here (both ligands are monodentate), think about what other property distinguishes a strong-field, strongly bonding ligand like cyanide from a comparatively weak-field ligand like water.
distractor_logic: Stability constants depend on ligand identity (basicity/field strength) as well as metal-ion charge and size; if only metal charge mattered, all Fe2+ complexes with different ligands would have identical stability constants, which is not observed.

Cyanide (CN-) coordinates through a single carbon (or occasionally nitrogen) donor atom per ion; it is monodentate, not didentate, so the chelate effect does not explain this particular stability difference.
Fe2+ does form recognisable aqua complexes such as [Fe(H2O)6]2+; the point being tested is not that this complex is impossible, but that it is considerably less stable than the cyanide analogue.

questions.question: In metal carbonyls, increasing pi back-donation from the metal into the CO antibonding (π*) orbital has what predicted effect on the C–O bond length and the M–C bond strength?
options: The C–O bond shortens (strengthens) while the M–C bond weakens
Pi back-donation has no measurable effect on either bond
Both the C–O and M–C bonds strengthen equally, with no trade-off
The C–O bond lengthens (weakens) while the M–C bond strengthens
questions.explanation: Electron density donated into CO's antibonding π* orbital reduces the effective C–O bond order, lengthening and weakening the C–O bond, while the same back-donation adds extra M–C bonding character (beyond the initial sigma donation), strengthening the M–C bond – the two effects work in opposite directions on the two different bonds.
questions.hint: Think about which bond's antibonding orbital is being populated (that bond weakens) versus which bond gains extra bonding character overall (that bond strengthens).
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual relationship; back-donation into CO's own antibonding orbital weakens (lengthens), not strengthens, the C–O bond, while it is the M–C bond that strengthens, not weakens.
Pi back-bonding is a well-documented effect in metal carbonyl chemistry, experimentally observable as changes in C-O stretching frequencies and bond lengths, so it is not negligible.

The two bonds are affected in opposite ways (one weakens, the other strengthens) due to the specific orbital (CO's π*) receiving the back-donated electron density; they do not both simply strengthen together.

questions.question: In Zeise's salt, K[PtCl<sub>3</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)], ethylene is a neutral ligand and each chloride is −1. Given the overall charge of the complex anion is −1 (balanced by K<sup>+</sup>), what is the oxidation state of platinum?
questions.explanation: Let the oxidation state of Pt be x. Summing charges: x + 3(−1) + 0 (neutral ethylene) = −1 (the overall charge of the complex anion), so x − 3 = −1, giving x = +2.
questions.hint: Set up a simple charge balance equation using the known charges of chloride and ethylene, and the stated overall charge of the complex ion.
distractor_logic: An oxidation state of +1 does not correctly balance the equation x - 3 = -1; solving that equation gives x = +2, not +1.
An oxidation state of 0 would mean the three -1 chloride charges are entirely unbalanced by the metal, giving an overall charge of -3, not the actual -1 charge stated for this complex ion.
An oxidation state of +3 would require the sum x - 3 to equal 0, not the actual -1 overall charge of the complex ion as given.

questions.question: Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>], is an effective anticancer drug, but its geometrical isomer trans-[Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] (transplatin) is clinically ineffective/less useful. What does this contrast best illustrate about coordination chemistry?
options: Platinum's oxidation state differs between the cis and trans isomers, which is the real reason for the activity difference
The two isomers actually have different molecular formulas, which explains the difference in activity

Geometrical isomers, despite having identical molecular formulas, can have dramatically different biological activity because the specific three-dimensional arrangement of ligands determines how the complex binds to its biological target (DNA)
Biological activity of a coordination compound depends only on its overall charge, not its geometry
questions.explanation: Cisplatin and transplatin are geometrical isomers with the exact same formula and the same Pt oxidation state, yet only the cis arrangement, with its two chlorides positioned adjacent to each other, can bind DNA in the way needed to disrupt cancer cell replication; this vividly demonstrates that geometrical (spatial) arrangement, not just composition, controls biological function.
questions.hint: Compare what is identical (formula, oxidation state, overall charge) between the two isomers versus what is different (the spatial arrangement of ligands) to isolate the real explanatory factor.
distractor_logic: Platinum is in the same oxidation state, +2, in both the cis and trans isomer; the oxidation state is not what differs between them.
Both compounds share the identical molecular formula [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]; they are true geometrical isomers of one another, not different compounds by formula.
Both isomers are neutral overall (the same total charge); since their charge is identical yet their biological activity differs sharply, charge alone clearly cannot be the deciding factor here.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of stability constants and the chelate effect, why EDTA is particularly effective as a chelation-therapy agent for treating lead poisoning.
options: EDTA is hexadentate and forms an exceptionally high stability constant chelate with Pb<sup>2+</sup>, due to the chelate effect, making the resulting complex thermodynamically very stable, water-soluble, and readily excreted, effectively removing free Pb<sup>2+</sup> from the body
EDTA works by lowering blood pH, which happens to precipitate lead salts
EDTA converts Pb<sup>2+</sup> into metallic lead, which the body then metabolises as an inert element
EDTA reacts with lead to form an insoluble precipitate that remains permanently lodged in body tissue
questions.explanation: As a hexadentate ligand, EDTA wraps around Pb<sup>2+</sup> forming multiple chelate rings, giving a very large stability constant (strong chelate effect); the resulting soluble Pb-EDTA complex is stable enough to hold onto the lead as it travels through the kidneys, and it is excreted in urine, effectively removing the toxic metal.
questions.hint: Connect two ideas: EDTA's denticity/chelate effect (which drives the large stability constant) and the practical requirement that the resulting complex must be soluble to be excreted, not just tightly bound.
distractor_logic: The mechanism of chelation therapy is complex formation (chelation) with the metal ion, not a generalised change in blood pH; EDTA's action is specific to metal-ion complexation, not acid-base chemistry.
EDTA does not reduce Pb<sup>2+</sup> to metallic lead; it forms a coordination complex with the ion as Pb<sup>2+</sup>, which is then excreted, not converted to a different chemical form.

A key requirement for chelation therapy is that the complex remains soluble so it can be excreted; an insoluble precipitate lodged in tissue would not remove the lead from the body and is not how EDTA therapy works.

questions.question: The IUPAC name "diamminetetraaquachromium(III) ion" is given. What is its coordination number and its likely overall charge?
options: Coordination number 6; charge +3
Coordination number 2; charge +1
Coordination number 4; charge +3
Coordination number 6; charge +2
questions.explanation: Two ammine + four aqua ligands (both monodentate, neutral) gives coordination number 2 + 4 = 6; since both ligands are neutral, the overall ion charge equals the metal's oxidation state, chromium(III), i.e. +3.
questions.hint: Add the ligand counts from the name to get coordination number, then note that neutral ligands contribute no charge, so the ion's charge equals the metal's oxidation number.
distractor_logic: This drastically undercounts both the coordination number (should be 6, from summing 2+4) and misreads the oxidation state (III means +3, not +1).
This undercounts the coordination number; 2 ammine + 4 aqua ligands sum to 6 donor atoms, not 4.
This gets the coordination number right but the charge wrong; since both ligand types (ammine, aqua) are neutral, the ion's overall charge must equal the Roman numeral (III), i.e. +3, not +2.

questions.question: A complex has the formula [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Cl]SO<sub>4</sub>. State its coordination number, and identify what type of isomer would result if Cl<sup>−</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> exchanged positions.
options: Coordination number 6; the exchanged compound would be an ionisation isomer
Coordination number 5; the exchanged compound would be a linkage isomer
Coordination number 4; the exchanged compound would be a geometrical isomer
Coordination number 6; the exchanged compound would be a coordination isomer
questions.explanation: Five NH<sub>3</sub> + one Cl gives coordination number 5 + 1 = 6. Swapping Cl<sup>−</sup> (currently a ligand) with SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> (currently the counter ion) to give [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Cl is the classic ionisation-isomer relationship.
questions.hint: First count donor atoms for coordination number (5 NH3 + 1 Cl), then recall which isomerism type describes an ion moving between the coordination sphere and the counter-ion position.
distractor_logic: This undercounts coordination number by only counting the five NH3 and forgetting the bonded chloride ligand.

This correctly gets coordination number 6 but misidentifies the isomerism; coordination isomerism needs two separate complex ions (a complex cation and complex anion) exchanging ligands, not a simple counter-ion swap as described here.

Linkage isomerism requires the same ambidentate ligand to change its donor atom; here, two entirely different ions (Cl- and SO4 2-) are swapping sphere position, which is ionisation isomerism, not linkage isomerism.

questions.question: A complex ion has coordination number 6 and is known, from magnetic data, to use d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization. If the metal is Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) and all six ligands are identical, is the complex homoleptic or heteroleptic, and how many unpaired electrons does the metal have?
options: Homoleptic; 0 unpaired electrons
Homoleptic; 4 unpaired electrons
Heteroleptic; 4 unpaired electrons
Heteroleptic; 0 unpaired electrons
questions.explanation: Since all six ligands are stated to be identical, the complex is homoleptic (only one kind of ligand). d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridization indicates a low-spin, inner-orbital complex, meaning the d<sup>6</sup> configuration is fully paired (t<sub>2g</sub><sup>6</sup>e<sub>g</sub><sup>0</sup>), giving 0 unpaired electrons.
questions.hint: Homoleptic/heteroleptic depends only on how many kinds of ligand are present; the hybridization type tells you the spin state and hence the number of unpaired electrons.
distractor_logic: This correctly identifies the ligand pattern as heteroleptic incorrectly (it should be homoleptic, since ligands are identical) though it does correctly identify the unpaired electron count for d2sp3.

d2sp3 (inner orbital) hybridization specifically corresponds to the low-spin, fully paired case (0 unpaired electrons), not the high-spin case (4 unpaired electrons, which would instead correspond to sp3d2 hybridization).
"Heteroleptic" would require more than one kind of ligand, but the question explicitly states all six ligands are identical, making the complex homoleptic, not heteroleptic.

questions.question: EDTA<sup>4−</sup> is hexadentate, giving [Ca(EDTA)]<sup>2−</sup> a coordination number of 6 from a single ligand ion. Explain why this single-ligand arrangement gives the calcium complex much greater stability than an analogous complex with six separate monodentate ligands providing the same donor atoms.
options: Hexadentate ligands cannot actually bond through all six donor atoms simultaneously, so real stability is unaffected
Coordination number has no relationship to complex stability

The chelate effect: wrapping one hexadentate ligand around the metal releases far more free solvent/ligand particles into solution than six separate monodentate ligands would, giving a much more favourable entropy change and hence a larger stability constant
A single ligand ion always has a smaller formula mass, which directly increases stability constants
questions.explanation: When one EDTA<sup>4−</sup> ion replaces six separate monodentate ligands (which would themselves have been displaced into solution), many more individual particles end up free in solution than complexed particles used up, giving a large positive entropy change; this entropy-driven stability boost is the chelate effect, and it is why hexadentate EDTA complexes are dramatically more stable than their monodentate analogues.
questions.hint: Think about the number of separate particles released into solution when one polydentate ligand molecule, rather than six separate monodentate ones, complexes with the metal.
distractor_logic: In practice, hexadentate ligands like EDTA do coordinate through all six donor atoms simultaneously in most of their complexes, which is precisely what gives coordination number 6 from one ligand and drives the strong chelate effect.

Coordination number, denticity and stability are closely linked concepts in this chapter; specifically, higher denticity (as in a hexadentate ligand) is directly connected to the chelate effect and increased stability, not unrelated to it.

Formula mass of a ligand has no direct, causal relationship to the thermodynamic stability constant of the resulting complex; the actual driver here is the entropy change (chelate effect), not molecular weight.

questions.question: The IUPAC name "potassium diaquabis(oxalato)chromate(III)" is given, where oxalate is didentate. Determine the coordination number of chromium implied by this name.
options: 8 (counting both metal and potassium contributions)
3 (counting only the number of distinct ligand types)
6 (2 aqua + 2 oxalato × 2 donor atoms each = 2 + 4 = 6)
4 (2 aqua + 2 oxalato, counting each oxalato as one donor)
questions.explanation: The name indicates two aqua (monodentate, 2 donor atoms) and two oxalato (bis-, didentate, 2 × 2 = 4 donor atoms), giving a total coordination number of 2 + 4 = 6, consistent with the "-ate" suffix marking chromium as part of an anionic complex.
questions.hint: Remember that "bis(oxalato)" means two oxalate ligands, each contributing 2 donor atoms since oxalate is didentate, not 1.
distractor_logic: Potassium is the separate counter cation, entirely outside the coordination sphere, and does not contribute to chromium's coordination number.
Coordination number counts donor atoms, not the number of distinct ligand types present; here there are 2 ligand types but 6 total donor atoms.
This undercounts by treating each oxalato ligand as contributing only 1 donor atom (as if unidentate) instead of the correct 2 donor atoms per didentate oxalate.

questions.question: Consider the two compounds named "pentaamminebromocobalt(III) sulfate" and "pentaamminesulfatocobalt(III) bromide". What is the relationship between these two named compounds, and how does their naming reflect it?
options: They are ionisation isomers; the name shows Br<sup>−</sup> as a ligand with sulfate as counter ion in the first, and sulfate as a ligand with Br<sup>−</sup> as counter ion in the second
They are the same compound named two different ways
They are geometrical isomers of the same coordination sphere composition
They are linkage isomers, since bromo and sulfato are both ambidentate
questions.explanation: In "pentaamminebromocobalt(III) sulfate", bromo is inside the coordination entity's name and sulfate is the separate counter-ion word; in "pentaamminesulfatocobalt(III) bromide", sulfato is inside the coordination entity's name and bromide is the separate counter ion – exactly the ligand/counter-ion swap that defines ionisation isomers, visible directly from which ion's name is fused into the coordination entity versus stated separately.
